The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot), during the discussion of the Post Office estimates on the 14th instant, called my attention to rumours of immense profits being made through the sale of stamps by the philatelic section of the department. To pre-

Privilege-Mr. Sauve

vent misunderstanding may I be permitted to quote from Hansard, pages 1723 and 1724. The hon. member stated:
Up until 1932 new issues were not sold through an agency, they were sold through the department; and if my memory serves me aright, in some instances amounts of $15,000, $20,000 and $30,000 were realized by the officials and paid into the treasury of this country.
The hon. member added:
At the present time any profit which might be gained through the sale of these stamps does not come to the government; all the government receives is the small amount it gets from the agency.
To this I replied, as reported on page 1723 of Hansard:
The philatelic branch has had a revenue of about $50,000 this year. It sells all stamps at face value. . . . They are not sold through an agency unless you call the philatelic branch an agency.
Further on the hon. member for Gloucester said:
To-day that revenue is nil, but those handling these stamps are making a fortune.
I then replied to the hon. member that if he wished to make a direct accusation of graft in regard to the sale of stamps, I would immediately look into the matter. The hon. member replied:
I did not say there was graft in the department. I said that the practice of the department led to graft to people outside the department but not in the department. I am not accusing the department of graft.
The hon. member added as reported on page 1725.
I want a definite answer to a question which interests the public as a whole concerning what to my mind is one of the worst principles ever established in the Post Office Department, namely, allowing outsiders to make a profit on the sale of stamps which should go to the government.
From the foregoing it may be inferred that the hon. member has clearly stated: That since 1932 the government has been deprived of some revenues by the fact that a philatelic section has been organized in the Post Office Department; that people outside the department have made immense profits through the sale of such stamps, and that the establishment of this section is "the worst principle ever established in the Post Office Department."
Since the hon. member claimed that he was not satisfied with the answer I gave on February 20 to the hon. member for North York (Mr. Mulock) and the further explanations given during the discussion of the

estimates, I promised to make a further inquiry into this matter. I wish now, with the leave of the house, to read a memorandum which will clarify the whole situation.
Prior to 1932 postage stamps sold to collectors were handled by the postage stamp division staff which also supplied all postage stamps to post offices. In view of serious criticisms made of the department that philatelists could not get proper information concerning stamps sold to collectors and also because the department seemed to be losing considerable revenue from this source, the work of the philatelic sales was organized in 1932.
No sale of unused stamps has been made under the philatelic section nor by the department since the philatelic section was formed, at more than the face value of the stamps.
In order that such work would be efficiently directed, this section, which forms an integral part of the organization of the department and is manned entirely by departmental employees, was placed under the direction of an official who had proper knowledge of such work and who could deal effectively with questions raised by philatelists. Since the organization of the philatelic section sales to collectors have averaged between $50,000 and $60,000 yearly and in the present year are expected to attain the highest figure in their history; the sales this year to date indicate a revenue of approximately $70,000.
Under the previous method of handling sales to collectors the average per annum was approximately $8,000 and the highest sale attained prior to 1930 was $30,000 in 1929. The revenue accruing from these sales has increased nearly nine times over any revenues received up to 1927 and has more than doubled under the present system the highest receipts prior to the formation of the philatelic section. The average sales for the past three years have been more than five times the overhead cost to the department, including salaries of the employees.
The department does not attempt to provide continuous sale of used postage stamps. A small quantity of such stamps is made available through preparation of these stamps for sale by an employee. When such stamps are available they are sold in numbers not greater than ten stamps of any one particular issue to one person, in order that collectors generally may have the privilege of obtaining them when possible, instead of allowing the whole supply to be bought in by dealers.
As shown in figures given in answer to a question asked in this house this year, the revenue for the last two fiscal years totalled

Questions
$155 from the sale of used stamps. Practically all used stamps sold to the public are sold by stamp dealers who obtain their supplies, not from the Post Office Department nor from any post office official, but from supplies salvaged from private sources. The Post Office Department does not deal in stamps having a known enhanced philatelic value, nor does it charge a premium on any stamps it sells. It sometimes happens, however, that stamps sold by the department at face value subsequently increase in their philatelic value, which has no relation to their value as postage.
The department has no official information regarding the prices at which these stamps are selling now to stamp collectors in the country, nor does it concern itself with such prices. The Post Office Department does not conduct its philatelic sales through any outside agency. All sales of stamps of any kind to collectors and dealers are made through the philatelic division of the department. All revenue from these sales is deposited to the credit of the receiver general of Canada on post office account, and becomes an integral part of post office revenue. There has been no deviation from this rule at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter just came to my attention a few moments ago, and I have just now been handed the answer to the question raised by the hon. member for East Hamilton, which with the permission of the house I shall read. It is in the form of a letter, signed by the Deputy Minister of Labour, and addressed to John McLean, president of the London Typographical Union No. 133, to whom the hon. member made reference. The letter is as follows:
Ottawa, March 18, 1935.
Dear sir,-The Department of Labour has recently received through Mr. J. F. White, M.P., and Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, M.P, the protest over the signature of yourself and Secretary Christie in regard to an article appearing on page 102 of the February, 1935, issue of the

Fisheries Act
Labour Gazette concerning .a strike of members of the International Typographical Union who were employed by the London Free Press and the London Advertiser
It is observed from your letters that the statement appearing on page 102 gives the information that the strike has terminated in favour of the employers. It is noted also that you desire to correct this statement and to emphatically say that the strike has not terminated. In support of your contention you point out that within the last two weeks a committee from your union has had meetings with the managers of the newspapers concerned and that negotiations are still in progress whereby an amicable settlement is hoped for.
In this connection I believe that if you will again refer to the article in question you will find that it does not bear out your protest, certainly not to the extent indicated in your letters. While the article does show that the strike has been recorded as terminated, that reference has merely to do with the departmental statistics. It 'will be observed that this particular reference shows clearly that the strike has not been called off or definitely terminated by the union involved. I am quoting hereunder the full text of this item:
" The dispute involving sixty-four members of the International Typographical Union and two daily newspapers in London, Ont., which commenced on March 1, 1934, the employers having refused to negotiate and sign a renewal of the union agreement, is recorded as terminated, the strikers having been replaced from time to time. The dispute has been added to the list in a previous paragraph of those in which employment conditions are no longer affected but which have not been called off or definitely terminated by the unions involved." This particular strike was carried for ten months as in effect, and as it appeared from information available that the strikers had been replaced the dispute was recorded as terminated in line with the general practice of the Department of Labour in such matters. This practice, I may say, is in accordance with the recommendations as to the method of compiling statistics of industrial disputes adopted at a conference of official labour statisticians called by the international labour office at Geneva in October, 1926.
I regret very much indeed that any misunderstanding has occurred in this respect, and I may assure you at once that in following our ordinary policy it was certainly not the intention to do any injustice to your local union. I am pleased indeed to know that negotiations have recently been resumed, and I desire to express the hope that the outcome will be satisfactory to the parties concerned. You are of course aware that the conciliation service of this department is readily available if desired.
I may add that your suggestion that the article to which objection has been taken emanated from or was influenced by the employers is of course entirely incorrect, as no communication has been received in the department from the employing companies on this subject.
Yours truly,
W. M. Dickson,
Deputy Minister of Labour.
John McLean, Esq.,
President,
London Typographical Union No. 133, London, Ontario.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, March 14, consideration in committee of Bill No. 21, to provide for limiting the hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day

Eight Hour Day
and forty-eight in the week, in accordance with the convention concerning the application of the principle of the eight hour day or of the forty-eight hour week adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization of the league of nations, in accordance with the labour part of the treaty of Versailles of 28th June, 1919,-Mr. Gordon (for Mr. Bennett)-Mr. Morand in the chair.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
When
this bill was previously before the house in committee last week it was passed with the exception of section 9, to which an amendment was proposed.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Was

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Yes. A
new section 9, embodying and overriding the existing provision, was at that time submitted to the committee. But objection was taken to it by certain members, including I think the hon. member for East Hamilton. Further consideration of the clause was postponed, and since that time a conference has been held between my colleague the Minister of Labour and myself, and interested parties, at which an arrangement has been arrived at. So I desire to withdraw the clause which was submitted as an amendment to clause 9 and to substitute therefor a new clause 9, the first portion of which is in the terms of the bill as printed and the latter portion of which is the amending portion. I should like to observe to the committee that this new clause 9 is based on article 5 of the treaty which I propose to read into the record:
Article 5
In exceptional cases where it is recognized that the provisions of article 2 cannot be applied-
Article 2 relates to the question of working hours.
-but only in such cases, agreements between workers' and employers' organizations concerning the daily limit of work over a longer period of time may be given the force of regulations, if the government, to which these agreements shall be submitted, so decides.
The average number of hours worked per week, over the number of weeks covered by any such agreement shall not exceed forty-eight.
The proposed clause 9 will read as follows:
9. The governor in council may, in exceptional cases where it is recognized that the daily limit of hours of work cannot be applied and agreements between workers' and employers' organizations to increase the daily limit have been made, give effect to such agreements and permit in such cases the said daily limit of hours to be exceeded: provided, however, that the average number of hours per week over the number of weeks covered by any such agreement shall not exceed forty-eight;-[DOT]
The following is the overriding proviso:
*-and provided further that in case such an agreement has been made prior to the thirty-first day of December. 1934, between a railway company and any employees' organization which embodies the basic principle of eight hours as the daily period of employment, the provisions of such agreement relating to the hours of employment shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this act, continue in force for a period of one year from the thirty-first day of March, 1935, unless suspended during such period by the governor in council.
The idea being to give a full year to the railway companies and the unions relating thereto having agreements with the railway companies to adjust their differences in the meantime. I may say that this is concurred in unanimously by the labour unionists there present.

I do not know then how
many railway organizations have stated to the government that they want an amendment of this character. All I know is that I have had communications in quite large numbers from railway organizations protesting that a forty-eight hour week is far too long a week in view of the large number of railway workers who are at present out of employment. We are going to give one year to the railway workers to adjust themselves to a forty-eight hour week, and the same thing applies of course to the companies. That is rather too long a time. At present when there are such large numbers of railway workers out of employment, who are anxious to find useful and productive work,
Eight Hour Day

I would much sooner see the time allowed for the change to be much shorter than the twelve months stated in the amendment. After all the number of railway employees affected by this legislation must be extremely small.
Second. I have an objection to this class of amendment I object to selecting one form of labour out of all the others and making special provision for it. I do not see why railway employees should be singled out for special legislation as contained in this proposed clause. There must be other classes of employment wheTe men may be affected, and we are merely opening the door here for exemptions under the bill which may be requested by other employees or employers who may be affected in exactly the same way as the railway workers are by this measure. Consequently, when we are attempting to pass legislation of this character, there should be equality in it, and there is not equality the moment we attempt to legislate for one industry and we do not legislate for others in exactly the same way. I realize that it may take time to adjust the position of certain classes of railway employees so far as hours of labour are concerned. The hon. member for Bow River informs me that under the bill as it reads at present they have three months, and with a large number of railway employees in the running trades out of work at the present time, when a man with twenty years seniority is probably wiping an engine or is not employed at all, or, as I know in similar instances, when such men are on government relief work, three months is a fairly reasonable time to allow railway employees to adjust themselves to the provisions of the forty-eight hour week.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
When the amendment was first suggested as an amendment to clause 9, it was made apparent that some time would have to be given in order to permit industry to adjust itself to the provisions of the bill generally. Then representations were made by organized labour, railway labour, the trades and labour congress of Canada, and discussions were held as late as this morning with the all-Canadian congress of labour. The various chairmen of the brotherhoods, some of which have many members who since 1928 have had difficulty in getting the work they would like on our railways, were consulted and the matter was gone into with great care. I recognize the dangers I have already pointed out in the debate of making a series of exceptions to a bill of this character, because of the everpresent danger of excepting the bill out of existence, if I may put the matter in that

way. But it must be borne in mind that for many years past railway workers in the running trades have arranged their agreements with the railway companies on a mileage basis. The various agreements-and there are many of	them-have	been
worked out on that basis during probably the past twenty-five or thirty years. Generally speaking the agreements have been satisfactory. I know that since 1928, by reason of various factors that have entered into the transportation business in Canada, a considerable percentage of railroad employees have been let out of the service or put on very short time. That is deeply to be regretted. Some of the factors causing that condition are beyond the control of any parliament or any railway company or any labour union. But the fact remains that the arrangements entered into voluntarily between the brotherhoods and the railway companies have grown up over a long period of years, and in the running trades have not been based upon an hourly schedule of work, but rather on mileage. These agreements are extremely complex, they are as complex as the transportation system itself. Having grown up over that long period of time, the representatives of all parties, both the railway companies and the brotherhoods and the labour congress, recognized that it was physically impossible to readjust within a shorter period than twelve months, agreements that would probably have to be entirely changed to an hourly basis rather than a basis of mileage or a combination of both, because it seemed to be the desire of those with whom I and my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce consulted, to spread this labour as far as possible amongst those railroad workers qualified to do the work. After the conference this amendment to section 9 was generally agreed to. Many drafts were made of the section in order that the difficulty which confronted us might be solved. Now, if it appears within a period of a year that these adjustments over the transportation system cannot be brought about, or if for any other reason the agreements are not adjusted in such a way that the greatest good will result to those most entitled to benefit, then hon. members will see that the amendment gives power to the governor in council to cause the suspension of the agreements or any one of them in the meantime. I believe that the amendment is the best that can be fashioned to prevent great confusion in the change-over from the present system to a system of employment that will fall within the principle and intention of the legislation.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION OP BODY TO COORDINATE WORK OF DEPARTMENTS AND TO INVESTIGATE AND ADVISE UPON SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PROBLEMS

speechtext:
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE PERLEY (Acting Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to establish the Economic Council of Canada and to provide for the employment of such officers and employees, and for the payment of such expenses as may be necessary to carry into effect the proposed legislation.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Morand in the chair.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION OP BODY TO COORDINATE WORK OF DEPARTMENTS AND TO INVESTIGATE AND ADVISE UPON SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The object of
this resolution is to establish a body to coordinate the work of the various departments of government and make more effective use of the ability and energy of the higher civil servants now in the employ of the dominion. I need hardly tell the committee that we have among our civil servants a large number of very high class men, men who are well-educated and capable in various directions
and who at the same time have an appreciation of the best methods and commonsense ways of dealing with things. They are students perhaps in the first instance, but the fact of their having been connected with the government here has given them other ways of looking at these things. They have a special knowledge of our economic problems, and we believe the setting up of this economic council, will, as I said, enable us to use their energies to better advantage, and will also save time and labour for members of the government of the day and especially of the Prime Minister. For this reason this economic council is placed under the Prime Minister.
It has been evident for many years that the ministers of the crown have too much detailed work to attend to, and that the Prime Minister especially under our system has far more to do than any one man should have. Many years ago when I was first a member of the government of Canada we talked over 1 his very question of the organization of the civil service and the work that was imposed upon members of the government, and the Borden government of that time decided to investigate this question. We looked around and picked out, we thought, the very best man that we could find in the world at that time to come here and give us advice on the subject. That man was Sir George Murray, who had been for many years the secretary of the treasury, the permanent head of the treasury in Great Britain, and who as everyone in this committee knows is the chief civil servant of Great Britain and their doyen. Sir George Murray spent quite a long time here and made an exhaustive report which contained very many useful suggestions. Among other things he was very definite in his statement that ministers of the crown and especially the Prime Minister undertook too much work and that it would be better if we followed a little more the system in vogue in the mother country of allowing the civil servants and the secretaries of the ministers to deal definitely with more questions than they were permitted to deal with here at that time.
Unfortunately the war intervened and, as was the case with many other matters, this report was lost sight of, so nothing has ever been done about it. That was twenty-three or twenty-four years ago, and since that time the work of government has vastly increased. My right hon. friend and other hon. gentlemen opposite who have belonged to the government, as well as my colleagues on this side, will agree with that statement. More
Economic Council

and more the government are being compelled to take cognizance of business questions and other matters which interest the country as a whole. Of late the newspapers have been referring to this, particularly since the Prime Minister has been under the weather. No doubt the Prime Minister's illness is due in large part to the heavy work he has had to carry on in the last four or five years. The newspapers have been commenting on this fact and drawing conclusions from it, with which in quite large measure I agree. It is believed that more assistance should be obtained from the permanent civil servants, and the bill I hope to introduce later on is intended to meet that situation to some degree.
This economic council can be given any work to deal with or any question to consider which the Prime Minister thinks it would be wise to have them look into. For instance, I fancy that everyone here will agree with my view when I say that perhaps one of the most difficult questions the world has to face to-day is the overgrowth of our cities, the fact that, naturally enough, people drift into the cities. That is due to the attractions of the cities, the bright lights on the main streets, the cinemas, the street cars and so on.

I have no doubt it would suit the hon. gentleman very well but I would feel sorry for the people if that happened.
At all events, Mr. Chairman, that occurred to me as an example of the type of question that might be referred to this council, the finding of some solution which would lessen the number of people in the cities and keep a

larger number on the land, not for the purpose of raising wheat or some other commodity for sale but for the purpose of making a living on the land, as our forefathers did and as the habitants of Quebec do at the present time. I fancy that would be a fair question to submit to this council which will be set up under the act I propose to introduce if the committee accepts this resolution. This bill has been preceded by a resolution because there is a small expenditure involved. That expenditure, however, really will be insignificant, since it is expected that those who serve will do so in an honorary capacity, and the functions of this economic council will be purely executive and not in any way administrative.
I fancy it is a platitude, Mr. Chairman, to say that the most pressing problems of the day are economic. We have provided for research in the natural sciences; some years ago we established an industrial research council, which is located in a fine new budding in the lower end of the city. But I think we may say that the next few years can be more profitably employed in research into economic science. It is true that of late years a great deal more attention has been given economic investigation. In many countries there are private agencies carrying on such investigations; in some countries wealthy men have endowed this research work under various foundations, and as we all know this work is being rapidly extended. In addition there have been governmental organizations of various kinds to deal with economic questions. During the last three years there have been full dress debates in this house on this subject, and I believe the last resolution dealing with it was introduced by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). I should like to congratulate the hon. member upon considering the matter as he has done and giving it so much study. This is an important matter and I believe all hon. members are grateful to him for bringing it up. When the resolution to which I have referred was under discussion in January last, speaking at the conclusion of the debate the Prime Minister said:
I do suggest to the hon. gentleman that the purpose he has in mind has been served, and while congratulating him and the other members of the house on the contribution they have made as to the value of scientific knowledge being applied to the nation and its affairs, as scientific ideas are with respect to the transaction of ordinary business by the various concerns carrying on the trade and commerce of the country, for those reasons I think the resolution might be withdrawn.

Economic Council
It would appear the hon. member for Red Deer agreed to the withdrawal of his resolution. We now have before us another resolution having for its purpose the betterment of conditions to which the hon. member referred.
Perhaps at this time I would do well briefly to review past policies and future requirements for the strengthening of our governmental machinery. Research falls into two sharply differentiated categories (a) research in natural sciences and (b) research in social and economic sciences. The purpose of this measure is to promote the latter aim, and is done if not wholly at least largely through the use of statistics. The term "statistics" has been defined as a science which treats of the measurement and interpretation of social and economic phenomena both as a whole and in separate manifestations.
A government is broken into various departments, each with a more or less specific function, and I submit that there is need for coordination and an omnibus point of view in economic policies. For the coordination of research in the natural sciences, the National Council of Industrial and Scientific research has been established. Similarly, on the economic side, which involves entirely different legal powers and technical methods, the coordinating problem was fundamentally attacked in 1918 when the Dominion Bureau of Statistics was set up.
In passing I believe it is only fair to say that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics has done first class work and must receive commendation from every person who has to do with it. This bureau supplies statistics which are absolutely trustworthy and available for every person. The policy of statistical research was inaugurated as the result of an inquiry made in 1912 by a royal commission. To-day however I submit to the committee that it is essential for us to go further and work from a wider and all-embracing viewpoint. This, we are doing in the present measure.
I believe between twenty-five and thirty countries have now set up bodies of this kind. They may be divided into two broad types or categories, namely those having more or less definite executive functions and those created for advisory purposes alone. These bodies are of various types, some being purely consultative and some having almost unlimited executive functions. The Economic Advisory Council of Great Britain was constituted in 1930 for advisory and research purposes only. It is given authority "to advise His Majesty's government in economic matters, to make continuous study of developments in trade and 92582-114
industry, and in the use of national and imperial resources. . . and of all aspects of national, imperial and international economy with a bearing on the prosperity of the country."
An economic advisory council is primarily an agency for inquiry and report. It is desirable to emphasize the point that it is not an agency for determining policy; policy must be determined by the government. It is not an agency for administration; administration must be the work of departments and commissions and does not fit in well with the central purpose of the advisory council, namely that of inquiry. While it should contribute towards a more considered and ordered planning of governmental affairs, is it not an agency for controlling the economic activities of the nation.
I have some references before me which, with the permission of the house, I should like to place on Hansard. These are extracts from reports which have been made regarding this particular matter. I find that in 1931 Sir Arthur Salter, who is director of the economic and financial section of the League of Nations, was consulted by the government of India with regard to the creation of a new economic organization in India. I quote the following from his report:
The period since the war has witnessed the development of what may prove to be an important adjunct to the machine of government throughout a large part of the world in the form of advisory economic councils and committees. These vary considerably in functions and in form; but they present certain common characteristics and seem to respond to a widely felt need in the post war world. The state's action in connection with the national economic life has almost everywhere become more extensive and more complex. Whether in the increased range of state control, or the construction of new and more complicated tariffs, or the institution of systems of prohibition or licence or state encouragement for some form of monopolies, the government has almost everywhere accepted more onerous and intricate duties.
I shall not read the whole of these observations. Skipping a portion of them I read:
The purposes vary largely, however, from country to country, and, with them, the form of organization. No system effectively serves them all.
(a)	The existence of a council composed of those with experience in every main sphere -of the country's economic .activity, established under legislative authority and, under varying forms, in effective contact with the government, often helps to secure greater coordination and unity of national policy. This is a real need because whatever the administrative organization of a particular government, most specific economic problems tend to cut across departmental frontiers.
Economic Council

That is to say, hon. members are aware that questions may arise which hold the interest of three or four departments of government Some way must be found carefully to consider the views of these various departments. Then to continue:
(b)	The new institutions may in several ways lead to an improvement of the statistical and commercial intelligence machinery which is available for the purpose of following the development of events and thought, both at home and abroad, and which thus affords a basis of statistical and other facts for the examination of current practical problems.
The report continues:
(c)	A third, and usually more prominent, purpose which is served, is that of securing the investigation of special economic problems, of current importance, by the _ best qualified experts including both economists and persons with business and other practical experience. This purpose is well illustrated by the British Economic Advisory Council.
In 1928 the Liberal Industrial Inquiry in Great Britain brought out a report entitled "Britain's Industrial Future" which contains a chapter warmly endorsing the idea of what is termed " An economic general staff." I quote from that report:
The problems of modern government have become more numerous and more technical. Parliamentary time, to an increasing degree, is occupied by questions which are primarily economic rather than political in the older sense of that word. Government departments have been subdivided and new administrative bodies have been brought into existence, not because of any bias towards bureaucracy, but by the sheer pressure of evolution in an industrialized nation. No matter how firm the determination of any government to avoid interference with industry, it finds itself called upon to remove difficulties from its path or to assist it. In any case, it is driven to recognize that in modern conditions its policies necessarily affect industry.
Nevertheless, the cabinet has no body of skilled advice on which to depend. The result is that troubles ahead are not anticipated, and, when they arrive, solutions to meet them are hurriedly improvised. Or, if competent commissions are appointed to_ study them, their reports come too late. Ministers and departments of state are necessarily concerned in the main with daily events and with the task of carrying On. The big problems of economic policy are only theirs when they are becoming ripe to be the subject of actual administration or legislation. It is, therefore, a vital need for a modern state to create a thinking department within the administration, which shall warn ministers of what is ahead and advise them on all the broad questions of economic policy.
As the problems of government become more technical, expert knowledge on them must be at the disposal of the government. It is not the duty of experts to decide matters of policy. But it is the duty of those who are responsible

for important decisions to make the fullest use of expert analysis and of expert statements as to the results which may reasonably be anticipated from this line of action or from that. It becomes more and more clear to the student of affairs, and indeed to the public, that many of the mistakes and blunders made by governments are due, not to ill-will or prejudice, but to sheer unpreparedness and' ignorance. A list of the major problems which governments holding office since the war have had to face illustrates the need of systematic thought in advance of executive decisions. There have been problems of a new kind as well as of unforeseen magnitude.
I omit the next clause, and would quote this paragraph:
Many of them are inter-departmental; and it has not been clear whose duty it is to exercise initiative or foresight.	What is clearly
required is that the cabinet should have at its disposal the best advice based on the fullest knowledge, and that the country as a whole should know that economic tendencies are not merely being recognized when some crisis occurs but that they are being constantly watched and studied, so that the government of the day may have a chance of averting difficulties and of meeting them with adequate measures.

May I ask what the
right hon. gentleman is reading from?
Sir GEORGE' PERLEY: Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear me; I am sorry. I am quoting from a report entitled " Britain's Industrial Future " made by the Liberal Industrial Inquiry in Great Britain in 1928. I have read those extracts to the committee because they show that this question has been receiving most careful thought in the old country, and I may add in almost every other country in the world. I submit for the consideration of hon. members these extracts that I have read, setting forth what seems to be a self-evident situation, and we hope that the arrangements that are proposed in this bill will help to meet these problems.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that with these preliminary observations the bill requires little explanation. When we go into committee upon it, I shall be glad to answer as fully as possible any questions that are asked. Although it is perhaps not in order to discuss the details at this stage I may say that the proposed bill sets up a council of fifteen, under the Prime Minister, recruited from three categories:	(a) government
officials; (b) representatives of organized economic bodies, and (c) experts. It may be that a good deal of the work of the council will be done by special committees created ad hoc which can work simultaneously on different problems allotted to them. This

Economic Council
will make it possible to keep down, the numbers of the council and to secure participation in its work by men who might otherwise not have the time to spare for a number of detailed inquiries.
The machinery which is in this way going to be provided will, we all hope, solve for some time to come what has undoubtedly developed into a prime need of government, that of keeping abreast of economic thinking in general and of being continuously equipped with the materials required in the formulation of its broader economic policies, and of having more definitely recognized machinery to that end. The plan outlined, we believe, by a combination of the pertinent features in other plans will avoid pitfalls which have been encountered elsewhere. Some of these attempts at economic councils have not worked out elsewhere as we would like to see them work out in Canada.
As I said before, this proposal involves a minimum of new machinery and expense. We believe it is an effort in the right direction and that it will produce good results. This suggested council, it seems to me, is important also because of the stimulation which it is hoped it will afford to private economic research; that is to say, private economic research will be encouraged to go on as well; and it is important also in view of the opportunities it will hold out to the universities and to students of economics at large for an understanding and a liaison with those who are on the council, and for thus uniting and pooling the results of economic thinking throughout the dominion.	*
It is expected that the cost of the council will be comparatively little. The services of the council proper will be honorary, and only a small clerical staff will be needed. Most of the work will be done by experts, who will be brought in temporarily in connection with the subcommittees to which I have already referred.
If this bill becomes law it is the intention to call the council together as soon as possible, and to undertake a program which will not only deal with broad and general economic trends but will also tackle a number of specific economic problems.
I have endeavoured, Mr. Chairman, to give the committee an idea at not too great length of the purpose of this proposed legislation and of what we hope will be accomplished by it. When we are in committee on the bill and hon. members have the bill before them I will endeavour to make any further explanations that I may be asked for.
