Mr. Chairman, I would prefer to wait until I see the bill which is based on the resolution before saying very much in regard to the proposal itself. I might say just a word or two now arising out of the remarks of the acting leader of the government, inasmuch as they give what purports to be the purpose underlying the measure, and to a certain extent provisions of the measure itself.
As to the purpose of the economic council which it is intended to create, I gathered as I listened to my right hon. friend that it was first of all proposed to be in the nature of an advisory body which would be able to assist the Prime Minister in the discharge of his onerous duties, and that it would come under the direction of the Prime Minister himself. There seemed to be the other purpose, which is that of research-a body that would be concerned primarily with research into social and economic questions-and as such would be made up of or avail itself of the services of members of the public service whose efforts and work would be supplemented by experts from outside.
Both purposes I think are not only worthy but necessary ones at the present time. I think there is need, in connection with the Prime Minister's office, of provision for more effective advisory assistance to whoever may be holding the office. I think also it is necessary at this time that some body should have as its special duty the work of research into economic and social questions. What I am in doubt about is as to whether these two functions can best be combined in the manner evidently intended in the bill that is to be introduced.
The acting leader of the government has said a word about my possible sympathy with and understanding of some of the duties of the person, whoever he may be, holding the office of Prime Minister. May I avail myself at the moment of such experience and knowledge as I had while in that office, to say just a word on this very proposal. What I think is not generally realized with respect to the Prime Minister's office is that it is the only office in which a minister of the crown finds himself isolated without assistance such as is to be found in other departments of government. The Minister of Railways, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, any other of the ministers of the crown when they are appointed to office find, on entering upon their duties, a highly trained staff immediately available. There is a
Economic Council

deputy head who in most cases has been familiar with the work of the office for years, there are important heads of departments; and there is the complete staff which is necessary to carry on the work. But a Prime Minister goes into an office in which there is no one and he is expected to be able to deal with questions of government relating to practically all departments, and to deal with great questions of state from day to day and, when parliament is in session, from hour to hour, and he has no one in his office to whom he can turn to assist him in that particular work apart from those who are referred to as his secretaries.
I would point out that the work of a private secretary to the Prime Minister ought to be much the same as the work of private secretaries to other ministers. It should not be work which will combine the duties of a deputy head, of the secretary of a department, and of expert advisers in different branches; it should be confined to those immediate duties which we commonly associate with the work of a private secretary. It seems to me that the handling of a Prime Minister's correspondence and the necessity of arranging for interviews, to say nothing of also interviewing persons who come to see the Prime Minister on various questions, are of themselves sufficient to absorb all the time which two or more able and efficient private secretaries can give. But over and above that which is a part of every day routine, the real work of the Prime Minister himself is with the larger questions of government which are related to world affairs and the affairs of different departments of state, and in that regard he is totally without the kind of assistance which other ministers have in their departments.
What is really needed in connection with ,he Prime Minister's office is the appointment of two or three highly trained and able men who possess qualifications and might be in a position to serve as advisers to the Prime Minister on the questions that are certain to occupy most of his time. Of these questions, undoubtedly social and economic problems will be one of the most important. But I doubt very much whether it will relieve the Prime Minister of the heavy duties of his office to have added to his other obligations that of being responsible for the work of an economic council which will be composed of fifteen persons, some of whom are in the civil service and others who are brought in as experts from without. A body such as that might more appropriately, it seems to me, be brought into relationship with the department
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
which now exists for the purpose of research. At the moment the national research council is giving its time primarily to scientific research; but why there should not be arranged, as a branch of that body or an allied body the kind of organization that is here suggested, I cannot see. I have in my hand a copy of the Research Council Act-

Does not
the leader of the opposition think that the type of research carried on by such a council as is proposed would be different from the type of research carried on by the National Research Council?

No, not as
to the machinery and organization required. In my opinion all research demands the same kind of qualities, and I think that the machinery or kind of organization found most effective for research in one-

But one
is deductive and the other inductive.

Both require
highly trained intelligence and those habits of research and processes of reasoning that are cultivated by men whose time and thought are given to study. They are different qualities of mind from those required for administrative work, but research into economic and social questions in what it requires of processes of reasoning is to my mind altogether similar to research in any other branch, whether it relates to medicine or any of the natural sciences or any other branch of knowledge. It is a branch of knowledge. I do not say that the same laboratories will be used. In connection with social science, the laboratory may be the country, the methods of study or research are the same. They are the methods of minute and detailed investigation with deductions therefrom. The methods followed in postgraduate study in the great universities include in some instances these very social questions and are wholly similar. The phenomena are different and the scope of inquiry may be different, but the methods of work are very much the same.
I favour the idea of a council or some organized body that will be engaged in research on social and economic questions, but I think it will function much more efficiently as part of the national research organization which has already been formed. I do not say that the officers need necessarily be the same. Let it be organized on its own. But to form a council and make it a body which the Prime Minister of the country must be

Economic Council
responsible for will, I think, add tremendously to the Prime Minister's obligations instead of relieving them.

I do not want to interrupt the leader of the opposition, but he has wide experience in organization work of this kind. I was going to ask him whether such a body could not be more closely related to the bureau of statistics which already carries out considerable special work.

What I was going to say was this, and the remark of my hon. friend bears out what was largely in my mind: If I were asked what would most assist a prime minister to-day in his onerous duties of government, I would say give him the opportunity to select two or three men in whose ability, judgment and discretion he has every confidence, have one of those gentlemen an adviser on social and economic problems and another to deal more particularly with state affairs that concern different departments of government and require the bringing together of the work of different departments in connection with matters on which the prime minister may wish to have the benefit of wider knowledge and advice, and allow those gentlemen to have a responsibility for using the public service in the way that will best serve the office of the prime minister. If the question is one of research into some matters of statistics, it should be possible for the prime minister to call upon the Bureau of Statistics to do whatever is needed for the government in connection with reports on statistical matters. If it is research into some other economic question, for example, the extent of wheat production and problems relating to wheat, it ought to be possible for the prime minister to call upon any department or group of officials of government to undertake that work. But I believe the work will be more effectively done, not by seeking to have one group or council which will have to deal with all classes of questions that may come up, but rather by having the machinery such that at any moment any particular branch of the public service may be drafted in to perform a special duty, supplementing its efforts by expert opinion from different sources.

Will the right hon. gentleman permit me for a moment? I am very anxious that we should see eye to eye in regard to the machinery for this council, and I may say, in regard to the last remark made by the leader of the opposition, that as I understand the matter, the problems of various departments will be dealt with in
that way and that what we may call ad hoc members will be taken on for the purpose of discussing and reporting on any particular question that has to do with Trade and Commerce or Agriculture or whatever department it may be. I think he will find the bill is all right in that respect.

Of course I am discussing the matter in a very general way and without any knowledge of the provisions of the bill. It may be that when we see the bill, some of my remarks will not be applicable. But what I am seeking to give to the committee at the moment is just the result of the remembrance of conditions as I experienced them when in office and as I believe the present prime minister has experienced them since he has been in office. To add to the present Prime Minister's many duties that of being responsible for the work of an economic council is not going to lessen, it is going to increase his duties, and for that reason I think any such action would be a mistake. But for this house to provide the Prime Minister of the country with two or three highly trained men in whose judgment he has confidence, who can be the instruments to help to bring to him the information that is needed with respect to great problems of government and who will be recognized as having authority to utilize the public services generally to that end, something of that kind would be of the greatest possible benefit. My right hon. friend is familiar with the position held in England for example by Sir Maurice Hankey. If we had in connection with our public service a gentleman holding a position similar to that which Sir Maurice Hankey holds, attached to the prime minister, a gentleman in whom the prime minister and ministers of the crown generally would have great confidence, who on behalf of the prime minister would be continually cooperating with other ministers of the crown in the assembling of material on matters that relate to great questions coming before the ministry for consideration, and who would be recognized as having authority to command the assistance of the public service generally, I believe such an official could be of tremendous help. But I do not believe a prime minister is going to be materially assisted by our increasing machinery for which he will be responsible. Where he will be assisted in a very real way is by giving him the aid of two or three men in whom he has every confidence, who will not be regarded as secretaries, who will not have the duties of stenographers, but who will be men of highly trained minds and intelligence and able
Economic Council

quickly to assemble and to assimilate the material which is needed for a discussion of public affairs. That would be the step which I believe would be most helpful' to a prime minister.
As to the other function-and I think the two have to be kept separate-of research into social and economic questions, I am wholly in favour of some small body in the public service being responsible for seeing that that kind of work is carried on continuously, and in accordance with known and proper methods, and of giving to a body of that kind an opportunity to add to its numbers from time to time with respect to the different questions that may come up. But I think such a body as that would be much better associated with a national council such as already exists, than it would be with the prime minister's office.
There is one other observation I should like to make at this moment, and it is this: I do not know what is contemplated in the way of appointments or staff, but while it may be alright for this house to consider the matter of machinery, and the provisions of a bill to meet the ends suggested, it would not be expedient before another parliament is elected for any appointments to be made to a body of this kind. The essence of the value of any advisory body is the degree of confidence that those who are responsible for its work may have in those who compose its membership. If the purpose of this bill is simply to enable the government to select out of different departments those who may be its particular favourites at the moment and to award them positions which are to continue for the next few years, then I say that the government is making a mistake in attempting anything of that sort.
Is not a still more important question the character of the investigations that they are to be directed by the government to undertake?

That is equally important, but there again that is a matter of ministerial responsibility. If this bill is intended to take away from the government its responsibility for the investigation of social and economic problems and to place that responsibility on the shoulders of some group to be specially named for the purpose as an economic council, then I think it will be but another step in the way of getting away from ministerial responsibility and I would not be in favour of it. I am not sure that the measure may not tend to have that effect. As we all know, throughout the world to-day there

is a tendency for governments to relieve themselves more and more of responsibility, and more and more to place responsibility on selected bodies for the purpose of re'ieving governments of some of their duties in public matters. If the measure is so intended I would think it inadvisable to have it enacted. A measure of this kind might more appropriately have been brought in at the first session of a new parliament rather than at the last session of an old parliament. But as it is coming at the last session of an old parliament, then so far as appointments under the measure are concerned they should be left until after a general election, when whatever administration may be responsible for carrying on the work of the government will have opportunity of appointing those for whose appointment they will have to be responsible and in whose judgment they will wish to have every confidence.

At this stage and without knowledge of the bill itself I shall speak very briefly; I shall not attempt to deal with what might be termed the machinery or the details. The suggestion itself I welcome in principle; that is, I welcome first the recognition by the government of the principle that economic and social problems are worthy of much greater and more concentrated study than has been given them up to the present, and second the principle that this can best be done by giving at least a degree of responsibility to a body of men to carry on that work. From the discussion so far I am not sure what will be the real form or functions or purpose of this body. It has been suggested that one of its chief functions will be to assist the Prime Minister. Well, I am in the fortunate position that I have had no experience as prime minister, and never shall have any-
Why not?

-but I have watched prime ministers in action, and I am satisfied, and I think it will be a sentiment agreed to throughout the entire house, that undoubtedly some assistance should be given to relieve any prime minister of the growing burden of detailed work which now rests upon his shoulders. I have not always seen eye to eye with the present Prime Minister; that could hardly be expected as I have always come into the house by defeating one of his supporters. At the same time I think I express what we all feel when I say, first, that we deeply regret the Prime Minister's illness and his absence, and second that we recognize that in large measure that absence has been forced upon

Economic Council
him by the fact that for the past four or five years he has been trying in all sincerity and in all courage to do two or three men's work.
Hear, hear.

Anything which will
take some of that load from the shoulders of any prime minister will be all to the good.
But as I conceive it the principal purpose in the formation of such a body as is proposed goes much further than that, unless indeed the function of advising the Prime Minister be interpreted in its widest possible sense. The Prime Minister is of course the head of the government, and advising the Prime Minister is in effect advising the government itself as to matters of major policy, placing before the government through the Prime Minister information necessary to enable that government to come to wise conclusions. Viewing the matter in that wider sense I assume that the function of advising the Prime Minister does include almost the entire functions of an economic council. It would be difficult for me to divide those functions into the two classes suggested, advisory and research. Advisory, certainly, but based upon what? Based upon the most intensive research into the problems, upon the widest possible knowledge and the most comprehensive study of the entire situation. I can conceive of no advice which would be worthy of the name unless it was preceded by and based upon that intensive research into the social and economic questions which I understand would be the first and primary duty of such a body. I shall not comment on the suggestion that has been made that to a large extent the body proposed by the present resolution will simply be an interdepartmental body to correlate the activities of various departments and coordinate the information which will be found therein. That would be a most useful function, but far from meeting the necessities of the case. However as that will come up in considering the bill itself, when the machinery will be discussed in more detail, and the method of appointment and principle of representation upon that council may be understood more clearly, I shall reserve comment upon that phase until that time.
I should like however to indicate very briefly some considerations which were before me and those who agreed with me when this matter was brought .before the house on former occasions, because as the acting Prime Minister has said this is a matter to which I have given some consideration. Indeed I think I have had the honour of introducing the suggestion in concrete form inito the house on
several occasions. I am glad to see those suggestions are bearing fruit. I may say at once that I am not so vainglorious as to believe that this bill is being introduced because I made the suggestion; at the same time there is a satisfaction in seeing that at that time I was interpreting public opinion and outlining a need, and that that need is now recognized in the house as well as throughout the country.
As to the work which might be doDe by such a body, the subject is so vast as to be approached with some trepidation, and touched upon only superficially in any address; and I have no intention of making an address at this time. I have on other occasions stated most of my general opinions on the subject. I listened with much interest when the acting Prime Minister mentioned one of the problems which might be referred to such a body, that of the trend towards the cities and the relative depopulation of our rural areas. While I agreed with him fully as he proceeded to indicate that the question of moving men into small self-supporting holdings in the country might be one subject of research, I thought if this were as far as the economic council would go in studying that problem it would fail utterly in its function.
Will the hon member permit me? That is only one points-

Oh, quite; I have no intention of suggesting that the acting Prime Minister limit the inquiry into the problem to that somewhat superficial aspect. I suggest that a study of that question must embrace most of the economic troubles that beset this nation, because you have to find out not only some way of distributing the surplus population from the city, but why there is this trend. The cause will be found to embrace the relative standards of living and the entire question of our industrial and distributive system, and to involve the whole subject of education and the varied opportunities which are afforded people in the rural and urban areas. I was disappointed-perhaps not disappointed but to say the least, surprised-rto hear the suggestion that that trend might be stopped were a change of government to take place. Any such suggestion shows a very shallow knowledge of the situation, because that trend has prevailed under every government and in every country. It was taking place with just as great acceleration in the nine years preceding 1930 as in the four or five years since; it is dependent on no special government being in power, and is far beyond any question of party politics. Its causes go far deeper than that; they go
Economic Council

to the very roots of our modem civilization, our industry and our agricultural system. I venture to suggest that in connection with that very problem the economic council would be obliged to investigate a subject which I think above all others should be investigated, the distribution in a proper way of that which we can produce and the relationship of finance and other factors to that distribution. This opens up a very wide field, and that is why I have in mind something perhaps a good deal more permanent and a good deal more important in the future than is visualized by the acting Prime Minister in this beginning. I quite realize the fact that the last session of parliament prior to an election is no time to set up wide and extensive machinery of any kind which might take over functions hitherto either unperformed or considered governmental. May I say at once that I only welcome this as the acorn from which a much larger tree may grow. I should like to see- and I hope this will be the germ-not a body composed mainly of departmental officials but a body truly representative of the problem itself, a body as permanent in its nature as the national council on technical and scientific research.
I am not going to compare those two problems. The acting Prime Minister has well said that economic and social research and all the problems related to that question are far more important and deserving of far more attention on the part of any government than are the problems of scientific research. The acting Prime Minister did not go quite that far, but that was the suggestion. I have said before, and perhaps it will do no harm to repeat it, that while technical and scientific research is carried on in many branches and in many places under private enterprise and initiative, because the results of that research may be reflected in increased profits, increased dividends or increased comforts to those engaged in the research, in the case of the corporations or firms carrying it on, properly speaking this question with which we are now dealing is one which affects primarily the state itself, society as a whole, not one individual particularly or primarily, not one firm or corporation, but the state as such. The solution of these problems would be reflected not necessarily in increased profits or dividends but in higher standards of living and better living conditions for the people as a whole. That means that there is only one body which should become primarily responsible for making that research possible; that body is the state, which represents all the people and society as a whole.
fMr. Speakman.]
I must confess, though I speak always with deference because of my more limited experience, that I cannot agree with the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the opposition that this council should be made a branch, as it were, of the present national council on scientific research. I agree entirely with the suggestion of the hon. member for Bow River; indeed I think I have made that suggestion myself, that while in one sense the problems are similar, there is a vast difference between the two. It is a question of knowledge and research and of the application of knowledge which 'has been obtained, but the methods are different, the subjects are different, the very bases are different. I agree at once that somewhat the same type of mind is required, that type of mind which, regardless of whose toes are trodden upon and regardless of how many existing prejudices may be upset, will search and delve until it reaches the truth and will bring in conclusions based upon that truth. I agree that the true scientific mind is required in both cases, yet I do suggest that the training of the mind and the objective are wholly different. More than that, the very basis is different. When you are dealing with scientific and technical research you are dealing with factors which may or may not be known but which, when found out, are tangible, immovable and certain; they are exact. In the realm of economic and social science you are dealing with something intangible, in regard to which differences of opinion will exist; you are dealing with questions on which at present few men agree. We have different schools of economic and social thought, and I may suggest that some of those schools of economic thought, some of those who are seeking a remedy for our present ills, hate each other worse than they hate the common enemy. So long as you have that frame of mind you cannot have the exact, scientific attitude brought to bear upon the problem which is essential.
Moreover I believe that the nature of the problem itself is so important and its scope so tremendous that it well deserves a separate establishment known and honoured as the national council of economic research, with its attention diverted to no other matters and with full power to carry on its activities. Further may I express the hope that we will see in this country not a body which will usurp the authority of parliament-I have never suggested that such an economic council should have the executive authority to put its findings into effect-but a body speaking with authority based upon knowledge, and after all upon knowledge alone can true authority be based. I hope this will grow

Economic Council
out of the present proposed legislation. I hope we shall have a body speaking with authority and taking the responsibility of advising the government as tj what policies would be most beneficial. Naturally any government and any parliament must take the responsibility of putting into effect and enforcing those policies. I am not suggesting in any way that the rights and responsibilities of parliament and of the government should be upset or usurped by any such body, but I am suggesting that governments and parliaments to-day are functioning, passing laws and taking action often on a basis of either ignorance or inexact and inaccurate information, and I believe this would do something to remedy that condition. I am not worrying just now about the welfare of any party, because I think after all that is a very trivial matter. I am hoping that out of this legislation as time goes on and as the idea develops, takes root and is accepted, as I believe it will be accepted, with acclamation-and the wider its spread and the deeper its roots the greater the acclamation-we may reach that point which we must reach or our problems will not be solved, that point when in parliament and out of parliament we can discuss these social and economic problems, which are of such overwhelming importance, on their merits, on a basis of knowledge and without the interjection of partisanship and political feeling. Perhaps that is too much to hope for, but at least it would take away some of the stigma and some of the stain of partisan politics if that information were at the disposal of the house and the government which must take the responsibility for introducing the legislation.
Perhaps I need say no more just now; after all this is only the resolution stage and I cannot tell, nor is it right for me to anticipate, to what degree and in what measure the legislation itself will bear out what I have said. In closing, however, may I say that I welcome this move because I see in it the adoption of a principle, the germ of an idea, which although it will be small this session, for good reason, perhaps may grow until it will form one of the most dominant and important factors in our modern civilization. The scope of the work to be done is enormous and the number of subjects to be investigated is legion. As I close I would suggest also that this is not merely a matter of searching out statistics and facts, important and all essential though those may be. I yield to none in my admiration of our bureau of statistics, which I believe to be one of the most efficient in the world to-day, much of its information
being useless because no use is being made of it. But if this were only a matter of delving into statistics and stating and correlating known facts, it would be but a barren move. Eventually we have to place on such a body the responsibility for the drawing of deductions and the correlating not only of facts but of opinions, and the responsibility for at least trying to think out something we have never thought out before, namely, what is going to be the final effect on the public weal of those different lines of isolated action. We have in Canada a number of outstanding illustrations indicating the need for a body such as I have described. I am not going to refer to that bete noir of the house, the transportation problem, nor shall I refer to many other matters. I should however like to mention one basic problem which may have caused more trouble for Canada than any other: I refer to the two divergent and conflicting policies which have been followed in Canada ever since western Canada was opened up. One policy encouraged by governments and by all who were interested in development was to make of western Canada a huge wheat exporting country. The western country was developed on that basis, and apparently every political party-and I am not now blaming the parties-parliament itself forgot that when accepting this as a paramount and foundation policy they were making of the west an agricultural country dependent upon huge exports for its existence. Side by side with that we attempted to build up within Canada the conflicting policy of a self-supporting industrial system. I submit that these two policies are mutually destructive; you cannot have both. Perhaps the source of some of our greatest troubles in making trade agreements and trade pacts and in getting reasonable tariffs, find their root in the fact that parliament went in two different directions, attempted to establish two different lines of policy, one of which was subversive of the other. You cannot have a country producing huge quantities of agricultural products, quantities normally in excess of its domestic needs, and at the same time have a self-contained industrial country which is not prepared to import the goods which must be accepted in exchange for the farm produce exported.
Again I am not suggesting that such a council should assume the responsibilities of parliament or of governments, but I do suggest that had a council been established many years ago and been given authority to make effective recommendations, the power to go into the facts and point out what would be
Economic Council

the results, the power to give guidance to parliament in what I consider was at that time a foolish and mutually destructive course of action, it might have prevented much of the disturbance and trouble we now find in Canada. One party in this chamber I am afraid cannot shake the finger of scorn at another, because the same policies have been followed by each and by parliament as a whole. Further than that, those policies have been supported by the people as a whole who thought they could visualize the ideal of a huge exporting country on the one hand and a self-contained industrial country on the other.
I suggest that is the kind of work which an economic council properly constituted and properly functioning might well perform. It could make suggestions to parliament and to government as to real lines of governmental and state policy which would result in reasonable balance and reasonably happy functioning. To-day one of the problems has been suggested by the acting Prime Minister, but the basic problem, that of making use of the abundance we can produce, to my mind lies at the root of our difficulties. This problem should be studied and examined impartially and free from partisanship or prejudice, so as to ascertain whether or not we may solve what has become not only a problem but a menace to ourselves and to civilization.

The resolution provides
for the appointment of an economic council. I say we already have one, because when I turn to page twenty-five of the parliamentary guide I find that we have first, the Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Secretary of State for External Affairs; second, Minister of Justice and Attorney General; third, Solicitor General; fourth, Minister of Finance; fifth, Minister of Railways and Canals, who is also in charge of tourist traffic; sixth, Postmaster General; seventh, Minister of Public Works; eighth, Secretary of State; ninth, Minister of Pensions and National Health; tenth, Minister of Marine; eleventh, Minister of the Interior and Superintendent General of Indian Affairs; twelfth, Minister of Labour, Mines, and acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization; thirteenth, Minister of Agriculture; fourteenth, Minister of National Revenue; fifteenth, Minister of Trade and Commerce; sixteenth, Minister of National Defence-and we have those very able men supported by a brain trust composed of three ministers without portfolio. First we have the acting

Prime Minister, then a former Prime Minister of Canada who is now leader of the government in the Senate, a man who is considered throughout Canada as a very able person, and third, another privy councillor from Prince Edward Island. Then, in addition to that we have another brain trust; there is the Canadian Minister to Washington who during the campaign of 1930 was the political adviser to the Prime Minister. Since then very often he has come to give his advice to the Prime Minister. In fact all this social legislation was inspired by him and was enunciated in his famous speech before the Canadian club at Ottawa. Therefore I wonder if the government will dispense with the services of such an eminent political adviser and replace by an economic council a man who is also an expert in the advertising of manufactured products. I wonder if the government would dispense with the services of such an eminent gentleman; I would be sorry for the government because he seems to be a genial adviser. I am pleased to note that the faces of the hon. members on the treasury benches are adorned with smiles. I know they are relieved; I know that this legislation means the former political adviser to the Prime Minister is now a thing of the past, and that he will be bound to remain in Washington, especially when questions are being asked about his travelling to and fro.
Then, in the various departments we have deputies and assistant deputies. These are men of great knowledge and wide experience. At times however the ministers are so well informed that they can dispense with their deputy heads. We find this happening in the Department of Marine and in the Department headed by the Postmaster General. These gentlemen have such wide knowledge of their respective departments that they can dispense with the services of their deputy heads. I would say however that every department is supposed to have a deputy head; that is in accordance with the law. It is a law which was good enough for Cartier and Macdonald, for Laurier and Borden and for Mr. Meighen. It was good enough for Mr. Mackenzie King, my right hon. leader. But now we come to this: We need an economic council. The government is eating soup for dessert because all the legislation on which the government should have had the advice of its economic council is already 'before us, and we have not had the benefit of the economic council's advice upon the social insurance measure, for instance, the eight hour day, and all the other legislation that is now

Economic Council
before us. Either that legislation is good or it is bad. if it is good, and I suggest that only for the sake of argument, we do not need that economic council. If it is bad, why was the1 legislation drafted before the economic council was formed? We are still living in a fools' paradise. I am sorry to 'have to say that, Mr. Chairman, but I cannot understand how the government can go on with this proposed legislation.
One hon. gentleman, I do not know wihether it was the acting Prime Minister, my right hon. leader or the hon. member for Red Deer, has said that this economic council is being formed as a measure of relief to the Prime Minister. The hon. member for Temds-couata has repeatedly in this house, and he has said it particularly to the Solicitor General, who is now listening, that the leader of t-he government should be given time enough to think by keeping away from him all those flatterers who make him waste his time by asking for favours. These good-for-nothings should not be allowed to approach him, in order that the Prime Minister may have sufficient time to think of matters of state. 1 have repeatedly urged that in this house, and I have urged it upon my hon. friend, and I ask him now to create a barrage between the Prime Minister and those who are making him waste his time by their visits.
It is not at all necessary for the government to have an economic council. May I quote from a book that was written by a French academician a long time ago, in 1909, His name was Emile Faguet, and the title of the book is Le culte de l'incompetence-The cult or the worship of incompetence. Here is what this author says at page 59 of this book:

That is the legislator:
II devrait etre tres inform^, non pas tant de ce qui est dans les livres,-quoique encore il dut avoir des connaissances juridiques assez etendues, pour ne pas faire, ce qui arrive a chaque instant, exaetement le contraire de ce qu'il veut faire-que du temperament et de l'esprit general du peuple pour lequel il fait des lois.
Le legislateur ideal, ou simplement suffisant, doit done connaitre les inclinations generales de son peuple et les depasser et les dominer, puisqu'il a pour mission en partie de les satisfaire, en partie de les combattre.
This resolution provides for an advisory council. In the time of Cartier and Macdonald-I will go further back to Lafontaine and Baldwin and say that we have had great men in this country, Lafontaine and Baldwin, Cartier and Macdonald, Borden and Laurier, my right hon. leader, and the right hon. leader
of the government in the Senate. All these were able men and they did very well without the assistance of any economic council.
Advisory? Why should this council be advisory? Why should the leader of the government receive any advice from people who are hair-splitters most of the time? There is no reason for such advice. May I bring to the attention of the right hon. acting Prime Minister, who is a graduate of Harvard and a well read man, this fact, that in the eighteenth century there was a strong tendency towards agnosticism in philosophy, but for some years now that tendency has been transferred towards the economic life of nations, and we now have a lot of cranks in the universities who are more interested in the solution of a theoretical problem than in the welfare of the people. Naturally there are exceptions, but there are many of those people I speak of, and we have to censure strongly some chancellors of universities, like one in Montreal, who is also the president of a great railway company. He tolerates in that university professors of economics who are socialists and communists and are teaching socialism and communism to the youth. The same thing is going on in Toronto university. The university I referred to first was McGill of Montreal, and the chancellor I referred to was Mr. Beatty, who does not object to some of the professors there, although they belong to highly respectable families, teaching socialism and communism to the youth. One of them is the son of a very great and a very intelligent man. I am in favour of freedom of speech but it is most dangerous to the welfare of the community and the future welfare of this country to allow those cranks to teach socialsim and communism to the youth. Why do we have so much trouble now in economics in this country?

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

The acting leader of the
government said that the object of this resolution was to establish a body to coordinate the work of the various departments and to make more effective use of the ability and energy of the higher civil servants now in the employ of the dominion. The civil servants at large are doing very well, provided that the minister is equal to his function. He adds that they, the higher civil servants, have a special knowledge of our economic problem. Is it not the business
Economic Council

of the government to have that special knowledge? They may direct the ability and energy of the civil servants along a certain line in order that they may make the best of the government's policies; but the special knowledge of our economic problems should be in the possession of the cabinet. The right hon. gentleman added that it would save time and labour to the government. It will save labour on the part of the government. But they must be ready to serve. If they are not satisfied with their task they have only one thing to do, and that is to resign and leave it to men who are not afraid to work. The ministers of the crown, he said, have too much detailed work to attend to. There is an easy remedy; curtail that detail work. It is a simple remedy, and it is because it is so simple that they will not accept it; they want something complicated. Let them direct their ability and energy to the welfare of the country. The right hon. gentleman referred to Sir George Murray, who had been the secretary of the treasury in Great Britain, and his advice to the Borden government twenty-three or twenty-four years ago. The fashion has changed since then. He continued : More and more the government are being compelled to take cognizance of business questions and other matters which interest the country as a whole. This is what we call in French verite de la Palice. It is most elementary that the government should take cognizance of business questions and other matters that interest the country as a whole; that is why they have been sworn as ministers of the crown and attend sittings of the council. The acting leader of the government said further:	The Prime Minister's illness is due in large part to the heavy work he had to carry on in the last four or five years. I do not deny that he has had a good deal of work, but everyone will agree with me when I say that he has had no system, and that is why he is exhausted now. No one compelled him to make long journeys to get a degree in the United States or in any province. It was tiresome and exhausting,, but the higher the degree the higher the fever. It was not part of the duties of the Prime Minister; he was supposed to stay here and look after the business of the state. I am sorry that he is ill, but if he exhausted himself travelling to and fro it is because no one on the other side, not even a doctor, gave him the very sound advice that he should stay in Ottawa and attend to his duties as Prime Minister instead of doing as a wandering Jew. fMr. Pouliot.]
The overgrowth of our cities is one problem which has been mentioned by the acting Prime Minister as a reason for this new legislation. Is there not a select standing committee on industrial relations and another one on agriculture? This matter could be studied at any time by either of these committees. There is no necessity to appoint such an economic council. The right hon. gentleman adds that one question that might be referred to this council is the finding of some solution which would lessen the number of people in the city and keep a larger number on the land-mark you this is most important-"not for the purpose of raising wheat or some other commodity for sale"-the farmer should not be on the land to sell his products; these are words which have been used by the acting leader of the government-"but for the purpose of making a living on the land, as our forefathers did and as the habitants of Quebec do at the present time." If they do not sell their commodities how can they make a living for themselves on the land? How can the farmer remain on the land if he grows commodities and does not sell them? It is most absurd, so absurd that it will take an economic council to devise a plan which will enable the farmer to stay on the land, to grow commodities which he does not sell. It is a most extraordinary thing, and I am sure that the idea was put into the right hon. gentleman's head by someone who wants to get on that economic council. The right hon. gentleman adds: "The functions of this economic council will be purely executive and not in any way administrative." We have already the executive council, which is the aggregation of ministers sitting in council. It is a part of our system along with parliament and the judiciary, and this will be done away with and will be replaced by an economic council which will have executive functions. It is easy to see that it will save time and labour to the government; it will do the work of the ministers. He adds that the purpose of this measure is to promote research in the social and economic sciences and that "there is need for coordination and an omnibus point of view in economic policies." It reminds me of the differences that exist between the former Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Secretary of State. I wonder whether the function of this so-called economic council will be to conciliate such divergent views in order that all gentlemen who do not share the same views will be put into an omnibus-an omnibus point of view in economic policies. It is a liaison body between all those on the other side of the house who

Economic Council
have divergent views; it is a matter of diplomacy. The acting Prime Minister quotes Sir Arthur Salter. That is a great concession to the group to my extreme left. Sir Arthur Salter may be a great economist, but his views can be considered in Canada not by way of application but only by way of comparison, because while he may know a great deal about problems in Great Britain, he knows nothing about ours. Therefore how can he apply his views? The right hon. gentleman adds that if this bill becomes law it is the intention to call the council together as soon as possible, and to undertake a program which will not only deal with broad and general economic trends but will also tackle a number of specific economic problems. The old order is gone; it is replaced by the new order as announced over the radio, but as soon as this economic council is formed, the new order will become the old order again and we shall have another new order created by these superlegislative brains. Are we to change like that all the time? Is this government's program a moving picture, changing several times a week? This is most absurd; there are no fundamentals in it. The government is very weak and needs some stimulant in order to carry on until we are bound to have an election. But it is very queer that in all the acting Prime Minister has said, there is not a single sound reason for creating such an economic council.
Now I come to what my right hon. leader has said. He says that the Prime Minister goes into an office in which there is no one, that is no staff, and he is expected to be able to deal with questions of government relating to practically all departments, and to deal with great questions of state from day to day and, when parliament is in session, from hour to hour, and he has no one in his office to whom he can turn to assist him in that particular work apart from those who are referred to as his secretaries. Then he observes that over and above every day routine the real work of the Prime Minister himself is with the larger questions of government which are related to world affairs and the affairs of different departments of state, and in that regard he is without the assistance which other ministers have in their departments. I am very sorry, but with that part of my right hon. leader's remarks I cannot fully agree. Did he mean that there should be a duplication in the Prime Minister's office of all the services that are in the other departments? Take for instance the bureau of statistics which comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce. The information that is gathered by that bureau is
available to every hon. member. I have nothing but eulogy for the excellent work which is done there; I am just a back bencher and I can get that information quite easily.
I do not see why the Prime Minister or the leader of the opposition has not the same opportunity, because the information is available to all of us. Therefore the Prime Minister or any hon. member can ask the bureau of statistics for any information which is necessary for him in his work, and I do not believe in any duplication of a service of that kind.
Then my right hon. leader says that to form a council and make it a body which the Prime Minister of the country must be responsible for will add tremendously to the Prime Minister's obligations instead of relieving them. Well, if it is a body for the Prime Minister, he must be responsible for it, and I am well aware that very often the Prime Minister has been advised by irresponsible persons. But there is enough of this and we cannot sanction it by a bill. We cannot as members of parliament give irresponsible assistants to the Prime Minister; I strongly object to doing so. The Prime Minister should be responsible for his staff just as any minister is responsible for his. Then my leader continues to the effect that for statistics it should be possible for the Prime Minister to call upon the bureau. He does not say it should not be possible. It is possible for the Prime Minister; it is possible for everyone. Then my leader says: If it is research into some other economic question, for example the extent of wheat production and problems relating to wheat, it ought to be possible for the Prime Minister to call upon any department or group of officials of government to undertake that work. It is possible for the Prime Minister to do so; it is possible for him to have that information at any time. Therefore, why create such an economic council? My leader says that to provide the Prime Minister with two or three highly trained men in whose judgment he has confidence, who can be the instruments to help to bring to him the information that is needed with respect to great problems of government and who will be recognized as having authority to utilize the public service generally to that end, something of that kind would be of the greatest possible benefit. That may be true. At the present time Mr. Finlayson is acting as super-secretary to the Prime Minister; he was appointed through the estimates. There are two ways to get the men referred to by my leader: either by submitting a request to the civil service commission or by inserting their names in the estimates. This
Economic Council

is a very easy way to do so and I do not see why the government does not proceed in that manner. If the Prime Minister needs more assistance and is not satisfied by that already given to him by Mr. Finlayson, let him put a name or two into the supplementary estimates asking that the House of Commons ratify the appointment of such men, and although such a proceeding is not regular, although they should be regularly appointed by the civil service commission, I would not raise an objection beoause I think the Prime Minister should have all the assistance that he requires to fulfil his duties. But on the other hand I do not see the necessity of such an economic council as is proposed by this resolution.
The hon. member for Bow River made a distinction between an inductive and a deductive body. The research bureau according to him is doing some inductive research. I wonder if I am quoting him correctly, and if I do not I shall be obliged to him if he will tell me. It is rather experimental than inductive work that is being done now by the research bureau and the hon. member knows that very well. Why make such a distinction between the inductive and the deductive? He knows very well that he is splitting hairs when he makes that very subtle distinction. On the other hand the new economic council will be a deductive body, a body doing deductive research. That is all right, but that work should be done by the government. That is why the cabinet meet; the deduction from the facts submitted to the government should be made by the cabinet ministers themselves when they sit in council. That is how they should frame their policies in connection with the business of the country.
I heard with a great deal of pleasure the hon. member for Red Deer mention something about the importance of facts. I have already told my hon. friends to my extreme left that they should be more interested in facts than in economists. Now they accept that suggestion in part; they do not accept it in full. They would like to have men in their statistical bureau doing the whole work for them in order to save them time and labour. That is what is suggested, because if I heard the hon. member for Red Deer aright, he said that someone should draw the conclusions from the facts gathered by the bureau of statistics. But that work should be done by the hon. member himself, as it should be done by the Prime Minister and his colleagues. When they ask information from the bureau of statistics they get facts and figures upon which they have to form their own judgment and draw their own 
conclusions. This is what a government is for; that is the idea of responsible government.
Then we are quite late in following other people's fashions. The brain trust was the fashion in the United States some years ago, but Mr. Moley was thrown overboard and later General Johnson, the head of the NRA, met with no better success. There is no longer a brain trust in the United States; President Roosevelt is getting rid of them. As the experience in our neighbouring country has been so unfortunate why should we follow that example now? In this house there are 245 members; representing every province and different parts of each province and each party. Members of all parties have the opportunity to meet members of the government or their leaders in caucus and there express their views freely, and to my knowledge members have often succeeded in changing the views of the leaders. This is the way that members of the cabinet can keep in touch with the members, and through them with the country at large. This is how it has been done ever since we have had responsible government. Not only that, but the ministers represent each province; they gather in council and discuss matters. The Prime Minister is the head of the Department of External Affairs, but he is more than that, he is the head of the. government, the superhead of every department; he is interested in the good administration of each department. He may get information through his ministers who gather it from every province. Furthermore the government can get information through this house. There are select standing committees, and committees appointed to study special matters, and information may be gathered by such committees from competent witnesses. The Prime Minister is the captain of the ship; he is responsible for the ship and for its crew and for the passengers. He has at his command these many sources of information-members of the house, officials of the departments, the ministers; therefore this so-called economic council is most superfluous and I will never agree to vote any sum of money or vote for any law to provide such relief for a moribund government.
There is a point on which I fully agree with my right hon. leader. He said that, as we all know, throughout the world to-day there is a tendency for governments to relieve themselves more and more of responsibility and more and more to put it on special bodies for the purpose of relieving them of their duties in public matters. That was putting it very mildly, but it is true just the same. The conclusion my right hon. leader arrives at is

Economic Council
that if this measure is so enacted he would think it inadvisable that it be enacted. I fully agree with my leader in that connection; I do not at all see the utility of this so-called economic council. All the government's social legislation has now been submitted to the house, or will be, except two measures. We know what it is all about. I do not see why we should bring in strangers and outsiders, people who have no responsibility at all, to advise the government; the government should be advised first by the members, then by the ministers; the ministers should advise the Prime Minister, the head of the government. If things had been done that way for the last five years it would have been much better and the government would not be in the jam they are in now. If the government had dispensed with all those intruders and that so-called brain trust the country would not have suffered as it has. Therefore, sir, I strongly object to this legislation. I consider it a farce. In my opinion its purpose is only to give a sinecure to some people who like to split hairs, who are not serious but are dreamers and cranks and a curse to this country.

I shall take only a few minutes, I hope. Someone has said that it is very foolish to criticize the architecture of a building without having first seen either the plans or the building. In other words to criticize before it is half-built is unlikely to lead to a right judgment. To criticize a bill when it is not even before us in skeleton form would seem equally unwise. Yet, judging by a remark dropped by my right hon. leader, there is a feature I do not like at all about this proposal, that is there are to be twelve or fifteen members of this "'brain trust" as my hon. friend called it. If that is so I do not like it at all. As anyone knows who has had experience in getting experts together, I do not care how expert they are, if you have fifteen experts you will have fifteen viewpoints and in the last analysis whoever is being advised has himself to take the responsibility of acting. This looks to me like an admission on the part of the government that they have not sufficient statecraft within themselves to administer the affairs of this country in these trying times; they have to call in people from outside. Well, they have done that on many occasions, but they were frequently unfortunate in their selection- of advisers. If I thought this plan would give them two or three good advisers and lighten the burden on the shoulders of the Prime Minister there would be something indeed much to be said for it. He has -been carrying a stupendous burden, but there is nothing in this resolution
to indicate that it is going to lighten his burden any more than that of other members of the government. As I understand it, it is an advisory body for the entire government, to be composed of some twelve or fifteen members. It seeems to be something in the way of a little Canadian pup begotten by the big Rooseveltian mastiff, a little NRA of our own.
That is the trend.

It is getting pretty well shot up down there, I understand; the mastiff himself is going bad. Why trail in at this time imitating our neighbours, big and wonderful as they are? They have demonstrated the weakness of this sort of thing. There are other ways of strengthening the government; probably the electors will have something to say about that.
You mean of changing the government.

Well, I would not like to be so unkind as that. I have had the privilege of acting under more than the one prime minister, both in the west and here, and I know what a ghastly grind it is, even on the ministers, but ten times more on the prime minister. If they keep at it long enough it will be only a matter of time until they break down, with the limited amount of expert confidential counsel available. I am one who puts the highest value possible on expert technical testimony, technocrats if you like; technical men I think are indispensable. But they often lack practical experience. I do not care how technical one is or how advanced he may be in the technical world; if he has not tried it out in reality in everyday affairs sometimes his technical knowledge will lead him astray, so he needs both the technical and the practical experience to be on sound ground as an adviser. If the aim of the resolution and the bill to be founded on it is to provide two or three advisers for the Prime Minister it should be possible to get two men with some technical knowledge, of course, but better still some common sense, some knowledge of statecraft, some knowledge of public sentiment, some knowledge of what will likely go and what will not go. I imagine any minister would like to have advisers of this type, as well as the Prime Minister.
There are two ways, as I see it, of carrying out the purpose of this resolution. My right hon. leader suggested that it might be done by having two or three technical men to assist the Prime Minister. That does not seem to
Economic Council

meet the wishes of the government, but though they have been known to change their minds it occurred to me that it was no use waiting until the bill came down to make suggestions; I might better assume that the bill is going to provide for a large number of advisers, some twelve or fifteen. Still I would suggest that the government carefully consider the other proposition of having two or three real good advisers, and not only advisers but assistants, who will help ease the terrible strain on the shoulders of the Prime Minister, no matter who he may be. That would be comparatively inexpensive; that is what has been done in the old country for many years. The idea of under secretaries in Canada has been mooted many times; that does not seem practical in this country, but this suggestion might be a substitute for that system, and it would help out tremendously and it would be inexpensive.
If it is desirable to have twelve or fifteen advisers why not do what has been done in the Department of Agriculture, not only by the present minister but by previous ministers as well? The minister calls his staff together, or he calls together farm organizations throughout Canada to meet in Ottawa. I think one of the first acts of the present Minister of Agriculture was to hold a conference with the various provincial ministers of agriculture, to take counsel with them. But you do not need a bill for that; you do not even need a vote in the estimates. On the other hand a vote in the estimates would provide for two or three experts without going through all this hullabaloo, but I think there is a reason for this more spectacular course. The government do not want the simple way; they want all the publicity they can get now, and I think perhaps they need it. The government want to pad out their rather meagre "reform" manifesto, and everything counts. This will be one more step to be tabulated off on their fingers, but this is going to cost too much, especially if we are to have a large body instead of the two or three advisers I suggest. The Prime Minister will have the burden, if he is the chairman of the body, of reconciling their differences. I do not know who will be the chairman, but whoever he is he will have to marshal the views of the other fourteen members, consolidate them and present them to the Prime Minister.
I am merely dealing with these points now because I may say quite frankly that if this measure goes through I will not want anything better on the platform than to describe the admission of the government that they have been unequal to the task of governing Canada, and that they are calling in an outside body for aid. So I am not making these remarks

for political reasons at all; I should like to save the government from themselves, and I think this is the time to do it. We have seen what has happened in other countries-the NRA for example-and we know what we have heard about technocrats. When this depression overtook us we had the views of every expert and statistician in the land within two or three months, and ever since they have been telling us the way out. In nine cases out of ten they have been wrong; the situation has been quite different from what they evidently anticipated, and they have had to back up and start all over again. So I have no very great hope in regard to this body of fifteen, since that has proven to be the case. They will be marshalled together from all parts of Canada and they will thresh out their differences. I have gone through that process more than once in a small way, and in the last analysis I found that I had to bear the responsibility and burden of working out something from the multitude of views brought before me.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, this will cost a good deal of money, and we have no money to spare to bulge out the staff at this time and call together these unnecessary large gatherings. As my right hon. leader indicated, the burden of being chairman of that body, or of being responsible for it, will take as much out of the leader of the government as it will save him. If you can get fifteen men together without some of them being freaks I tell you you are a good chooser. The danger will be that one or more freaks will be chosen; they are the people who will assert themselves. Some of our Major Douglases and what not probably will be on this body but of course good men also. When I make these remarks I am not attempting to belittle the responsibilities and1 labours of a prime minister. There is no one, unless it is my own leader, who knows better than the Prime Minister the need of good, straight, honest outside advice by two or three men of common sense, horse sense if you like, and perhaps some technical knowledge. Such advice is of tremendous help, and I should like to see something done to make that advice available to whoever happens to be prime minister, because I am conscious of the need of it. Any further remarks I have to make, Mr. Chairman, will be deferred until I see the bill.

I should like to make
a few remarks on the resolution that has been debated this afternoon and this evening, but first I have a question or two to ask the right hon. gentleman who is piloting the resolution through the committee. I should

Economic Council
like to ask what will be the extra expense to parliament and the country when this economic council of fifteen is established?

I explained this afternoon that the expense will be very small. The bill will provide that these men will act in an honorary capacity. I do not think any estimate has been made as to what the expense actually will be, but I can have some estimate prepared and give it to my hon. friend when we are in committee on the bill itself.

You cannot give an
approximate figure at the present time?

I say that the
time to discuss a matter of this kind is when the bill is in committee.

Then we will leave it
at that, and we will expect that information later on. Now I have another question to ask the right hon. gentleman. This afternoon he spoke of the secretary of the British treasury, Sir George Murray, who came to Canada when Right Hon. R. L. Borden was Prime Minister. My right hon. friend did not give the year. May I ask him now exactly what year he was referring to?

I think it was
either 1912 or 1913.

You are satisfied that
it was 1913?

It was either
1912 or 1913.

I wanted to know, because in discussing a measure of this kind it is important that the man leading the government should know all the details. They constitute a good foundation of any resolution.
Now there are just two or three thoughts I have to express, and I do not intend to delay the committee very long. We were told this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman leading the government that the work of this economic council of fifteen members will be first to correlate the work of the various departments of government and second to get more physical and mental energy on the move. Having told us that the council to be set up was to be made up largely of civil servants, he pointed out that the name economic council was to be given to the newly-established body. If we are to have as a foundation of this economic council some of the experts of the different departments I should think the name civil 92582-115
service council would be more applicable than the name economic council. Apparently the civil servants are to be robbed of any credit in respect of name to be derived from the measure, and a new name is to be given. However, that is not very much to bother about. We will wait until we see the different clauses of the bill, when it is brought down to find out why this aspect of the matter was overlooked.
May I say it is not necessary to have an economic council to get the work of the different departments better correlated. It is not necessary to have an economic council to get more work both physically and mentally out of the different departments of the government. I should think that that correlation and that accomplishment of more work could be got just as well by the cabinet of the day led by the Prime Minister. The machinery is there; why not organize it? Why have the country pay for more machinery? Why not organize what you have and get one hundred per cent efficiency out of it? If that were done it would be absolutely unnecessary to have this measure.
I agree with the hon. member for Melville when he states that the very idea of adding to the bureaucracy of this country and adding greater financial burdens to the different provinces and the country as a whole will be all the argument necessary in western Canada to show and prove that the present government has lost the confidence of the people largely because it cannot meet effectually and efficiently the problems which confront the country with the machinery at their disposal. That is the situation.
One more thought:	The suggestion was
made this afternoon that the Prime Minister has become incapacitated and has got into his present condition of ill health because of too much work. I am one who wishes that the Prime Minister may be in a condition as soon as possible to return to his parliamentary duties. We need a real leader at the head of the government, a man with plenty of energy and ability. The Prime Minister is possessed of these two qualities, therefore I say that the sooner he is back the better for parliament and for Canada. May I say that if the Prime Minister has broken down-if any prime minister would break down under the load of government he would be called upon to bear at present- the fundamental fact is that when any one man tries to run the country as prime minister entirely apart from his cabinet, the probability is he will break down. Greater cooperative use should be made of all the

Economic Council

elements and members of the cabinet. Every man should be asked1 to do his duty departmentally. If that were done the load of the Prime Minister would not be as heavy and, in the present instance, the breakdown might not have occurred. Further, not only should theTe be more cooperation among members of the cabinet, not only should there foe more solidarity, more correlated effort and more individual activity which would have the effect of releasing the Prime Minister from many of his duties and responsibilities, but there should be more organized effort in his department, and perhaps in every department of the crown. If that were done I believe the Prime Minister could give more attention to the serious part of government and thereby give a more efficient lead to the party in power, irrespective of which party it might be.
One more thought, and then I am through. When the matter was under discussion this afternoon the right hon. gentleman placing the measure before the house and explaining it touched upon the trend to the cities from the country. He said the bright lights were one cause, the cinemas another, the street cars another, and so on. These are only the external causes.
Stop the street cars.

The right hon. gentleman did not go into a detailed analysis of the real problem; he left out the basic part tff the picture. Because of that one hon. member to my left said, "Why not admit high tariffs as a cause?" High tariffs has been one of the causes which have led to the drift from the country to the' city. They surely are. Any person who reads the history of the last fifty or sixty years will see that the trend is from the country to the city, and if he analyzes that economic trek he will find out sooner or later that the cause is really in the high tariffs which have been placed upon the primary industries in Canada, and have had the effect of bankrupting those industries to such an extent that the people on the farm do not choose to remain there, simply because they cannot get a decent living. Many of them are on relief to-day. As I said, when the matter was before the house one hon. member to my left asked, "Why not accept high tariffs as one of the causes of this population drift?" That is one view of the question. Following that remark I suggested, "Why not change the government?" The hon. member for South Perth a while ago asked a similar question. When I made the suggestion the

hon. member for Red Deer took a holier-than-thou attitude with regard to it and soared into the clouds, delivering a kind of lecture to any person who would have the temerity to talk about tariffs and a change in government. He made out that he had something deeper, wider, longer, and more important in every way to tell the house.
I was referring not to tariffs but to the Liberal party.

The hon. member states he was referring to the Liberal party. Well, as I was going to say a little later the contact between hon. members opposite-in a word, the Conservative party-and the hon. member for Red Deer was clearly demonstrated to-day. He withdrew his former resolution, and now we find the government taking action upon it. The two are uniting in the establishment of this economic council. May I say, or may I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Red Deer is out afteT a position in the present government? Is he trying to get one- of those velvety chairs in the cabinet or brain trust of this government?
Pretty mean.

I do not know whether he would be accepted or not. We do know the resolution he moved was withdrawn, and now the government has accepted the principle of it. I should think that establishes a point of contact between the two parties, and no one knows what may come forth in the future. History might repeat itself. I would say to the hon. member for Red1 Deer that if he wishes to lecture anybody he had better lecture himself and the members of his own' party-
