-since he and others of his group stood up in this house and voted for high tariffs. He has voted for high tariffs in his own province, and to-day he gets up in this house and discusses a resolution of this kind without even mentioning the important element, namely, high tariffs. I do not think that will be very popular in western Canada. I know it will not be popular in Saskatchewan at all events.
I would say, Mr. Chairman, that if the hon. member for Red Deer is no more correct in his diagnosis of this resolution than he was on the poultry and egg pools, then he is very far astray indeed. I understand that he takes the attitude that he knows more about the marketing act than the Minister of Agriculture himself, and more about the egg pool

Economic Council
and more about the poultry pool, and I am wondering whether the Minister of Agriculture is taking it for granted that it was because of the hon. gentleman's identification with the marketing board policy that the thing was put out of business in Saskatchewan, in Manitoba and in Alberta-given a knock-out blow, as it were.
These, Mr. Chairman, are a few rambling remarks that I wanted to make on this resolution.
Oh, oh.

They are rambling to a oertain extent because the impetus that was given to them came, as it were, from a rambling member of this house. In conclusion I would just say that in my humble opinion the trend to the city from the country is almost entirely due to high tariffs, and until those restrictive tariffs are modified, Canada's national and international trade will remain at a low ebb and the drift to the city will continue.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he rejoices in the fact that the marketing act was, as he says, defeated in western Canada ?

It is not necessary to
answer that, Mr. Chairman, because apparently the vote in Manitoba and in Saskatchewan and in Alberta shows that the people there are rejoicing over the result. So what more do you want?

I understand that the
members of the cabinet have so much work to do that they feel feeble and exhausted and need some outside assistance. If they are feeble and exhausted on account of their labouring pains may I suggest to them that they take beef, iron and wine. It is an excellent tonic and will make them strong and well. But besides that, instead of a brain trust, they should use brain food.

Mr. Chairman, if all the hon. members who wish to speak on this resolution have done so, I should like to say a few words in reply to what has been said by the hon. member for Melville and also by the right hon. leader of the opposition.
The hon. member for Melville, I was glad to note, thinks that this is really a reform measure and one that is brought down for the purpose of bettering the condition of the people. I hope when he goes out into the country and speaks to the people, he will inform them accordingly. I was also rather surprised to hear him say that you 92582-1151
could not get a council together of fifteen men without having some freaks. I would like him to rise and tell me who was the freak in the last Liberal government, if it is true that you cannot get fifteen men without having one freak.
He is too modest to name himself.

The right hon.
leader of the opposition referred to Sir Maurice Hankey and the work that he has done in England. I knew Sir Maurice Hankey very well when I was over there during the war as high commissioner, and a very splendid executive he is. He is a civil servant in one sense of the word I suppose, but he acts as secretary to the cabinet. Contrary to our method here they keep minutes of the cabinet meetings in England. We do not do that here.

You
could not.

I did not catch that. I want to inform the right hon. leader of the opposition and the committee that although Sir Maurice Hankey fills a very important position over there, at the same time they have an economic council as well. With the right hon. gentleman's argument, that the Prime Minister should be provided with one or two specially selected men to help him in his arduous duties, I am in entire agreement, but I am not prepared to say that these secretaries could absorb the duties to be performed by this economic council.
The right hon. leader of the opposition also stated that in his opinion the scientific and industrial research council might take up this work. I do not agree with that at all. I consider that the work to be done by this economic council is entirely different from that which is being done by the scientific research council. I am not criticizing in any way the work that is being dome by the research council at the present time, which I am told is very useful and helpful, but it is an entirely different type of work and requires a different type of mind. The scientific research council is concerned with investigations and experimentations. That is their job. The duty of this economic council on the other hand will be to apply the information that has been gathered by that other council.
How?

The council is to consider everything that is being done in the way of improvement.
Economic Council

But in
the last analysis it can be applied only by parliament.

I know that the council is only advisory, but it could review all the information in connection with mechanical and scientific progress that has been obtained in the last fifty years and consider how it could be used to better the conditions of the people. So it seems to me that they are two entirely separate and different kinds of duties, and I hope that the right hon. gentleman upon further consideration will feel that way himself.

Mr. Chairman, may I say one word before this resolution carries? Broadly speaking I do not share some of the general criticisms of this resolution which have been voiced by some of my colleagues on this side of the house. I have always believed in a general way, and have so stated many times on the platform, in the principle of an economic council, but while I say that I want to make some reservations. I do believe that if there is any value whatsoever in an economic council, that value should have been seized upon by this government in 1930 immediately after they came into office. But as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Temiscouata we have had this administration composed of some seventeen ministers proceeding on their way for four and a half years without taking any advice whatsoever from any outside party, and now, just on the eve of an election, they seek to buttress up a very weak position by the creation of this economic council. It is well within the knowledge of every single member of this house that the trend of the world in the last five years has been towards the creation of boards and commissions and tribunals and economic councils.
Bureaucracy.

It is the new despotism, the new bureaucracy. If I may venture into the unsafe realms of prophecy, I would say that just as the tendency of Canada and other nations in recent years has been to detract from and impinge upon the fundamental authority of free democratic parliamentary institutions and create all the boards and commissions we have seen-the tariff board, the marketing board, the radio commission, and all kinds of tribunals and boards of trustees-so in the future those who will succeed us in this and in other parliaments will I believe have to fight to reassert once
[Sir George Perley.3
more the fundamental authority and responsibility of parliament, and abolish all these evils of bureaucracy.
I am supporting this resolution. I believe if there is any advice that any government can obtain from any outside body of economists in these days, that advice should be freely asked and freely given and freely taken advantage of.
I understand from the remarks of the acting leader of the government that this economic council is to consist of fifteen members with the Prime Minister as chairman. It will probably represent all the varied commercial and business activities of the nation. I wonder what authority this body will have. Unfortunately for the sponsors of the measure they will not be here to dictate to the new body which is to be created under this legislation. But suppose my hon. friends opposite were in power when this body commenced to function-

They will
be; don't worry.

That lies beyond the kindly veil of the future. Would * this economic council have authority to deal with the most important questions confronting Canadians? There are two things to-day which are completely unscientific. In the first place, our tariff structure is altogether unscientific. Would this council have any authority, seeing that hon. gentlemen opposite have themselves created the tariff board, to investigate the tariff structure of Canada and make recommendations to the cabinet?
Apparently not.

The second most unscientific structure in Canada, a structure which has been built up seetionally over the years, is the freight rate structure. Would this council have authority to make specific recommendations to the government with respect to changes in the Canadian freight rate structure? The third point is this. We have a marketing board, or rather nine or ten marketing boards. Would the council have authority to interfere with the jurisdiction of the marketing board in the marketing of natural products? Again, by far the greatest problem in the dominion to-day is the immediate solution of our difficulties in connection with the debt. What about the debt structure and the coordination of financial responsibilities and of dominion authority with the various provincial authorities? Would your economic council have power to-morrow to investigate the assets, revenues and expenditures not only of

Supply-Privy Council
the federal structure but of all the various provincial structures in Canada and to make specific recommendations to the government?
The argument used by some hon. gentlemen in regard to relieving the administration of responsibilities does not seem to me to carry weight. I am strongly in favour of the creation in Canada, no matter what government is in power, of a system of under secretaries to the ministers of the day, who shall be trained to study all questions of the hour and who will directly-not inferentially or indirectly-relieve the tremendous responsibilities that devolve on those who are charged with public office. I believe that sooner or later you must devise a system along these lines. So that so far as relieving the responsibilities of the Prime Minister or of any minister of the crown is concerned, I do not believe that the argument for an economic council is a weighty one. If my right hon. friend will assure me that he will summon without emolument, as the measure seems to indicate-only expenses will be required-the most brilliant men to study the great questions of income and outgo with respect to the expenditures of the government, to study the great questions with regard to our railways and our freight rate structure, to study questions with regard to the tariff, and then to make recommendations in an advisory capacity to the cabinet, leaving the final authority and direction to parliament, then I think I can see some merit in the suggestion made in the resolution. But I agree with my hon. friends who have spoken, that this is only one more step in the mad race towards despotism and bureaucracy which the government has been running since 1930; and some day those who succeed us will be very glad to come back and restore to parliament complete control over the destinies of the Canadian people.

Has the minister's attention been called to the prices of both hogs and cattle in the United States as compared with Canada? A year ago we were reminded of this frequently at a time when the price was lower in the United States. Now it is considerably higher. Our cattle are going to Chicago now instead of to the old country. I do not think that any live hogs have gone to the United States but bacon will be shipped
if prices keep up. I have no recollection of the United States having an Ottawa agreement.

There are very considerable shipments of cattle now from this country to tihe United States owing to the fact that their cattle prices are so much higher than ours, high enough to take care of the very high duty they have placed against our live stock. The increase in the price of their live stock chiefly their fat live stock, is due to a number of causes, and perhaps the first is that there is a great area which has been affected by drought in the United States, extending from the Canadian boundary. In October I drove from Regina straight south, and along an area of over 800 miles in the United States, due north to due south, there was no green vegetation of any kind that could be seen, and that extended in some places from 400 to 500 miles on either side of the line. The effect of the drought was so bad that the American government took vary drastic steps. After investigation they felt that it would not pay them to ship fodder and other feed for live stock over the great distances that would have to be traversed, and they took steps to slaughter some of the cattle on the ranges and purchase large numbers, having them canned for use as far as possible among people on relief. As far as my memory serves me, the percentages are these. In Montana, the Dakotas and some of the other northern states the number slaughtered was as high as 51 ver cent; that is, one animal out of every two slaughtered. Some were left where they were slaughtered and were disposed of there. The others, as I stated before, were converted into canned meat and so on, and a good deal of this is still in storage in the United States. Other states slaughtered as much as 47 per cent; in Oklahoma, further south, the quantity slaughtered was 41 per cent. This will give the committee a good idea of the very large number of cattle slaughtered, the proportion being over one-half in some of the states.
I am speaking now from memory, but the total sum of money expended by the United States federal government in purchasing those cattle was, so far as I remember, more than
8108.000.000. More than 8.000.000 head altogether were slaughtered, and of that number, in the neighbourhood of 1,450,000 odd were slaughtered on the ranges. There were two factors connected with the matter: one was that as a result of the drought there was a shortage of feed which raised the price of feed for cattle in the United States. On the other hand at that time cattle were very

The area affected by drought was nothing like as large as that in the United States; only a few thousand head of cattle in Canada were destroyed to be used otherwise than for human consumption. But during the past four or five years, that is since 1929-30, the United States government put up the tariff against Canadian cattle, and because that outlet was denied to our cattle, our surplus increased very greatly. This last year I believe we slaughtered between 350,000 and 400,000 head more than we did in previous years, the farmers holding their cattle hoping that some action might be taken to allow them to enter the United States and avail themselves of that market if it might rise, and the old country market, which was practically the only one available and had reached very low prices, might also rise. 'But because cattle were low in price and feed was high, there were few cattle put on feed in Canada in comparison with previous years.

Coming back to the fairs, I was wondering whether the minister could give some information regarding the success of the regional fair policy. I intend to make just one comment in respect to it; I have watched the operation of one such fair. In attempting to establish regions around a central point, no matter how well you try to handicap the inside area, the outside areas further away do not seem to be able to enter sufficient stock to bring their prize list up to a point where they can make enough to have winnings really to pay their way. With transportation quite uncertain, the experience that we have had has been that it takes tremendous amount of persuasion to bring some of these people from outlying districts into a regional fair to compete as a region. Would the minister be good enough to tell the committee just what success these regional fairs have been having and what the policy with respect to them is going to be in the coming years?

As the hon. member for Macdonald has stated, it is difficult to make a fair adjustment between the advantage to those near where the fair is held and that to those in more outlying districts. The success depends pretty much on the natural location of the fair selected as a regional one as to other smaller communities, villages, that are around it. It also depends a great deal on the type of the exhibition board. In some cases where the exhibition

board of the regional fair take a highly personal interest in it, they can work up a great deal of competition. In that way we think it is very valuable in comparison with the old system of fairs that took place for many years and finally reached the point where they had a cut and dried prize list and did not have to put much individual effort into the work. It is rather difficult to make comparisons because conditions have been so abnormal, but I would say that on the whole the expression of opinion from those who have taken advantage of regional fairs has been very valuable as to how they work out the regional idea in their own districts.

There is a report that our
cattle going to the old country have been found suffering from disease. Has the department any information on that question?

When the restrictions that were placed against our cattle were removed at the time of the Ottawa conference agreements, so far as female stock, especially that which was to be used for dairy purposes, was concerned, we agreed with the United Kingdom that any animal which they felt was not suitable, not of high enough quality to be used for breeding purposes, could be slaughtered. In addition to that however- and perhaps this is what the hon. member has in mind-some few months ago there were shipped to the United Kingdom dairy cattle that were not in proper physical condition to ship and that were not good specimens of the breed or anything like a good advertisement for our live stock in the old country. We advised the exporters a number of times that it was necessary to take steps to prevent the shipment of those cattle, because we had reports from the old land, with reference to one shipment especially, that if further shipments like that were made there would be danger of an embargo being put on lest disease from these animals should spread in the old country. As to the last shipment, about which there has been something in the press, the reason given for the slaughter of those cattle was chiefly that they were not of sufficient high quality for breeding purposes. The female stock are tested here for tuberculosis but not other diseases.

Can the minister say
whether or not the cattle reported in the press to be diseased and unfit for breeding purposes were examined by competent veterinarians before they left Canada?
For general disease yes, but the only specific test I understand was for tuberculosis.
Can the minister inform the committee if all the space that was required for cattle offered for export to the British market last fall was available?

We had no information as far as I know from any individual that there was any considerable lack of space. There were some isolated instances of inability to get space; one was from the vicinity of Biggar, where I believe there were two or three carloads. Mr. Clark, I believe, wrote me in connection with it. I believe one of the chief reasons in that case was that he did not give as definite a commitment, as was required, as to when he would want to ship. From the reports that came back I think it might have been better if there had been even less space available, because on the shipments as a whole I understand there was a substantial loss.

Is any attempt made by the department to control or distribute the space1 that is available for cattle exports to the British market?

This is a large item, and I would like to draw attention to the fact that the grants to fairs are given to fairs in the larger cities, but under present conditions a great many farmers, in fact the average farmer, finds it impossible to get to those cities to visit the fairs. Therefore it seems to me that the smaller fairs should be more liberally treated.
I should also like to know what percentage of our cattle are exported, and if the price received for that exportable surplus sets the price for all cattle in Canada.

Answering the last question first, my answer would be no. My information, which I have every reason to believe is accurate, is that on the whole during the past two or three years the cattle shipped overseas have brought less than similar cattle sold in the domestic stock yarns.
With reference to grants being increased to fairs in the smaller centres, we have increased grants more in such centres than in the larger ones, for the very reason the hon.

member suggests. At one time the grant to fairs in the larger centres was $5,000; that was cut practically in two, I believe, while we gave some additional grants to some of the smaller fairs. This year there has been an increase to B fairs to $1,800 plus 1200 for defraying expenses of judges, and $500 for regional fairs, plus $500 if used for junior farm work, which is a greater increase in proportion than to the larger fairs. I agree entirely with the statement of the hon. member that we cannot afford not to encourage the smaller fairs which are more available to many farmers than are the larger ones.
What roughly is the percentage of cattle exported?

The number of cattle exported is between fifty and sixty thousand. The number slaughtered at inspected packing plants is somewhere close to 800,000 I believe, and that is considered to be about half the number slaughtered in Canada, so the percentage would be very small.

The minister mentioned just now the necessity for killing off live stock in Canada and the United States. Last summer in our section we had a bumper hay crop, and we were expecting to get fairly good prices. But we were told that the federal government had put an embargo on the shipment of hay to the United States in order to keep the price fairly low for farmers in western Canada. I would ask the minister if that is true.

I am glad my hon. fried has raised that point, because there has been a good deal of misunderstanding about it. In the first place, due to a shortage of feed in the United States, they took the tariff off hay and straw going into that country provided it went into the areas which have been affected by drought, where feed was necessary, but only when it was imported through certain agencies. So the tariff was not taken off except under very specific conditions. Representations were received from western Canada that a shortage of hay and straw and feed for cattle was expected there; there was also an expected shortage in the province of Nova Scotia. For that reason it was felt desirable that exporters should be licensed to export hay and straw from this country so that in Canada we would not suffer from any shortage of feed and the people who bought hay and straw in this country would have to pay a price equal to that at which it could have been sold for export. With the exception of the first five or six or perhaps ten days, though I think for a shorter period than that.

when there was some misunderstanding in reference to this matter, no person who had an order was refused permission to ship either hay or straw out of this country. So I do not feel that any person was adversely affected, except that possibly certain buyers felt that there would be a very excellent market in the United States, and at the beginning, before the situation became well known, they did go through the country stating that they did not know whether they would be able to get the feed out of Canada, and I believe they did persuade some farmers to sell to them for next to nothing. Any cases that came to our attention were followed up, and so far as we know no person suffered (hardship in that connection.

Is it true that the federal government helped the provincial government feed the cattle in the dried out areas? Is it true that the federal government, through their own agencies, bought some hay or other fodder in the eastern sections of Canada and shipped it to the west?

So far as feed goes the federal government has not absorbed any of the cost. We have absorbed some of the freight cost in connection with moving cattle out of these areas. My information is that no hay has been bought in eastern Canada and shipped to the west. The freight rate would make the cost prohibitive.

That matter has
been given consideration each year. We realize that many of the cattle that have gone to the old land have not been of the quality we might have wished, and have not been a credit to the best cattle in this country. The first year in which I looked into this matter personally I was given some very interesting information by Mr. Brown, who at that time I believe was purchasing well over seventy-five per cent of all the cattle we were exporting. He purchased and paid for them on this side of the water, and his emphatic opinion was that while if we shipped all top cattle they might bring more than the cattle we did ship, every person did not want to buy top cattle. He said he had a cargo of perhaps five hundred head consisting of two or three different grades, and that there was always some person on the market wanting a lower grade, another wanting a little better grade and another wanting a choice grade. I know Mr. McKenzie's views very well; I had a visit with him in Toronto shortly after his return. What he said is perfectly true; we would get a better price for our cattle if we shipped better cattle, but investigation has shown that we get a substantial increase in price over there as compared to what we would get here, for some of our very commonest cattle.

I would like to ask the minister to explain to the committee why on the English market our bacon obtains practically the lowest price of all the bacon offered for sale on that market, and why, with our steadier supply-and we must have a steadier supply because we are shipping more-the price is not better in relation to the bacon of other countries.

There are a number of factors that contribute to the lower price. In the first place we cannot ship a steady supply. The hon. member knows that, in western Canada perhaps more than in the east, the farmers have certain farm practices, depending upon the season of the year and the best time to have pigs born. The result is that the great majority of the pigs are born during two periods in the east and one period in the west, so there is a gap that naturally results and which could be avoided only by giving some assurance to the farmers that during that period a premium would be

paid for their hogs. For example, in 1934 there was one very large distributing house in the old country that had worked up a large trade in Canadian bacon. They found themselves in August, September and October, and particularly in August and September, unable to obtain a sufficient supply to meet the demand they had been able to create. That was due to the fact that with the prices here compared to the prices over there, due to the practice of having pigs come at a certain season of the year there was a gap in the supply.
I agree with the hon. member that this is one of the most important problems confronting us to-day in connection with the bacon industry. In wheat we have no such trouble, because there is always a supply available. The only way I can see to overcome that situation in regard to bacon is either to have the packers combine and say they will pay a certain premium to eliminate that dip, or for the farmers themselves to combine and work out some scheme, such as a very small levy to be used to set up a fund, so that when that time comes they can keep the supply going forward that we have led the people over there to believe would be sent forward. I do not think that could be considered a bonus; it would be contributed by the farmers themselves and would be more a process of levelling up.
Then my hon. friend referred to the fact that our bacon brings a lower price than other bacon marketed in the old country. One reason for that is that Canada is a country with varying climatic conditions. Another reason is that people have gone into the business of raising pigs without having raised them in the past, and they are not as expert as they should be at finishing them or at getting the best type. Many of them sell their pigs when they are underweight, thereby leaving smaller sides. In the old country there has been a surplus of smaller sides, and for that reason we have not been able to put over as uniform an order as otherwise we would have done. Also the bacon finishing is not evenly done in different parts of the dominion. I make haste, however, to correct any impression I may have given that our farmers have not made the very greatest efforts to improve the quality of our bacon. The fact is that in the last three years the quality has improved from fifty-one per cent to sixty-one per cent in selects. Another factor has been that in the last year in particular there has been a shortage of feed not only in western Canada but in Ontario. That shortage has put many

farmers in a position whereby they could not finish their pigs as well as they might wish, and they had to get them off early.
There is a great demand in Canada, too, for choice bacon, and this demand has to be met. When the market in the old country was opened up, giving us an advantage and an opening for the marketing of a high percentage of our high quality bacon, some of the supply had to be taken from the market we had established here. I can assure the hon. member, however, that we are very closely in touch with the situation, and for further assistance we have appointed a special officer who, before going overseas, visited the packing plants in Canada. He has gone to the old country and has done very excellent work in examining large shipments of our bacon which have gone over there, and has reported back as to the weaknesses, indicating how our product has fallen short of the requirements of the old country.
To standardize the quality of bacon sent out of Canada we have passed regulations whereby only inspected bacon may be exported. That does not mean that every piece of bacon is inspected, but it does mean that the standards are well known to the packers. Certain boxes or bales a-re inspected, and if we find there is a tendency to ship bacon below standard, very severe penalties, going to the extent in extreme cases of the cancellation of licences, may be imposed.

Does the government
grade our bacon which is shipped out, and are the top grades shipped? In other words, is the best grade kept in Canada?

There are three
grades of Canadian bacon, practically only two of which are shipped, as the third is negligible. Our information is that the bacon shipped is in accordance with the grades. It is difficult to define the grades because of the different practices obtaining in the different packing plants. To get anything in the way of uniformity of standard it was necessary to have a number of meetings of the packers. The result was that they investigated more carefully than they had done before the practices of curing bacon. They visited each .other's plants, and the result was that it was discovered one plant which as a rule may not have had as high quality hogs as other plants was turning out a more uniform product. For that reason their product was more acceptable. I believe one reason for their success was that they had machinery similar to that used in Denmark. The result of the meetings was that various packing plants

changed their methods of processing, so that to-day we believe we have a much more uniform type of product for export. The packers are frank in their admission that that has done more than anything else towards standardizing our product.
Then, in reference to grade, careful consideration was given to the desirability of having our bacon gain the best reputation in the old land. It was felt the best procedure would be to set a very high grade. The officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce in the United Kingdom and some of the officials of the Department of Agriculture who had visited the United Kingdom, together with people who had marketed their products over there, were of the opinion that if we put only the very top grade on the market, and that if we exported only the best quality of our bacon, we would get a certain result, but that if we sold a large quantity of our second grade the tendency would be a discrimination against Canadian bacon. All these points have been considered very carefully. We feel that on the whole what we have done has been in the best interests of our bacon market. There is, however, a great deal still to be desired in getting across a uniform product with a uniform finish and in a steady flow. No effort is being spared to achieve that end.

The impression seems to have gone abroad that our packers are shipping out an inferior quality bacon, and that they set the price for hogs in this country by the price they obtain in the old country. Naturally that is a lower price. Some people have the idea that that is the reason a lower price is being paid in Canada for hogs than should be paid.
I should like to ask the minister what has become of a certain variety of hogs which was brought from Sweden only a few years ago; I refer to the Landrace hogs which were brought to Canada. How many did the minister buy; what has been the increase in number; what price did he pay for them; where are they now; and are they registered? Further, I should like to have a general idea of what is being done with them, and if any tests have been made.

We expect that about next Saturday there will be an increase ; I know, because I was out looking at them to-day. Sixty-seven of these hogs were purchased in Sweden. Negotiations were first conducted in Denmark, but the people of that country apparently did not seem anxious to ship hogs of 'that quality to their competitors. Our officials finally proceeded to Sweden and in that country were able to make satisfactory
negotiations to have a shipment of the hogs sent to Canada. So that there would be no danger of bringing any disease with these animals, instructions were issued to have them quarantined at Quebec for six months. After that time they were brought to the experimental farm at Ottawa, where they are now There are fifty-one females at the experimental farm, and it is our intention to have them thoroughly tested. Their gains will be watched, and an accurate record of the feed given them will be kept until they reach a weight of about 220 pounds. They will then be slaughtered and their carcasses valued in points, figured on a certain number out of a possible hundred for a perfect carcass. Perhaps the outstanding difference between these pigs and our own Canadian Yorkshire or white pigs is that the pigs imported have smoother shoulders. Their sides run more smoothly into the shoulders than obtains in the average Yorkshire pig. They are also deeper, on the whole, and their heads are smaller. The aim is to have the side form the greatest possible proportion in the weight of the whole pig. Although great improvements have been made in the matter of increasing the length of the Yorkshire pig, that length has been achieved at the expense of the ham, while the shoulder has been left practically the same. It will be of interest to know that in both Denmark and Sweden the only selective process is brought about by actual feeding. Prize winnings at exhibitions do not mean very much. That is why last year we started throughout Canada testing stations for the same purpose. Some of these pigs that have been imported from Sweden have thirty generations of tested ancestry behind them. Many were imported from Denmark to Sweden, and Sweden has made a very scientific job and keeps a very scientific record. So we feel we got the very best pigs possible.
I know the question in the hon. member's mind is, when will they be distributed? None of them will 'be distributed until they all have been put on test to see how they respond to the climate and the feeds of this country. We may carry out our crossing experiments with Yorkshires. They may be sent out in groups throughout the country. Many of those who opposed this importation because they had been successful breeders of Yorkshires now are among the strongest advocates of the course we took in bringing over this shipment. We are not doing anything in a haphazard way. Every care will be taken to test them before they are distributed.

I understand that there has been some grading of hog or bacon carcasses on the rail. What success has that met with?

We have been carrying on for some time experimental work in testing carcasses on the rail, and last year we decided to cany out this work more extensively, starting first at Peterborough and Kitchener. The result has been that practically every person there now wishes his pigs graded on the rail. They feel that by so doing they get the exact value of their pigs.
There has been no opportunity of testing the value of rail grading so far as export is concerned?
No. grading for export is entirely independent of that.
The minister mentioned a moment or two ago the grants made to tihe A and B class fairs.
The grants to the B class fairs have been increased to $1,800 and an additional $500 has been made available for competition at these fairs for junior farmers, boys and girls and junior farmer clubs.

Is it not a fact that an investigation which took place into the Land* race hog in 1909 and 1910 found that the Yorkshire hog was in many respects better than the Landrace and better even than the cross bred? It was found that it took more to feed the Landrace hog per pound of pork produced than either the Yorkshire or the cross bred, that t'he bacon on the prize animals came from the Yorkshire instead of the Land-raoe or from the cross between the two, and that in practically every respect the Yorkshire was the superior hog to the Landrace for bacon purposes.

There has been no investigation in this country as to the Land-race hog and the Yorkshire hog because this

is the first time there have been Landrace hogs in this country. We cannot say yet which hog is most suitable for our climate and our feeds. Perhaps what the hon. member has in mind is that some years ago Denmark used to import large numbers of the large white or Yorkshire hogs from the United Kingdom. They used them to get their pure bred sires and for one cross with a view to improving their bacon. As time went on they made investigations purely from a dollars and cents point of view, and they have now entirely quit the importation, or practically so, of these large white hogs, and are now using not only for bacon purposes but for breeding stock ninety per cent I would say of LandTace hogs. That I believe is our best answer for the shipment here.
